speechtext: On May 16, during the debate on the war appropriation resolution, I called to the attention of the Minister of Public Works certain inequalities with respect to salaries and war supplements paid to firemen working under the jurisdiction of the minister's department. At the time he was good enough to indicate that he would inquire into the matter to see if any injustice was being done, and undertook to remedy it if he found that to be the case. The war appropriation bill having been passed, and no answer having so far been made, I should be very glad if the minister would acquaint the house with the result of his inquiry and tell us what he proposes by way of remedy for the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works

Mr. Speaker, the leader
of the opposition was good enough to give me notice of this question. He is right in saying that during the discussion of my war estimates he inquired about the salaries paid to the seasonal firemen employed by the Department of Public Works. I intended giving the information when my civil estimates were before the committee. However I have now before me a report concerning the 118 firemen employed at Ottawa.
The salary range of these employees is from SI,140 to 11,260 a year, plus the cost-of-living bonus and in certain instances a war duties supplement. In the case of firemen it was found that some fourteen employees, due
IMr. A. L. Macdonald.]
to the increased work caused by the war, were now filling positions which under the rating schedule I have mentioned would qualify them for stationary engineer grade 1, and these employees were recommended to receive the minimum of that'class.
In addition, statutory increases not ordinarily accorded to firemen were granted. These were authorized on recommendation of the department by order in council P.C. 144/2200 of March 28, 1944, effective April 1, 1940; and these increases are now in effect and also apply to firemen outside Ottawa.
Of 118 firemen at Ottawa, fourteen received war duties supplements, three received $120 statutory increases and twenty-four received $60 statutory increases. Thirty-two will receive stautory increases in 1944, when they will have served two seasons, and thirty-eight in 1945. Thus there are only seven firemen who have not been benefited, and they were already at the maximum of their class.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext:
The whips of the various parties have decided to place me in the farthest corner, so that I am sometimes forced to speak louder than others have to speak.
(Translation): I wish to point out certain injustices contained in this bill. Unfortunately, it was moved at the last minute last Friday, and by referring to the record it is found that it was passed almost without discussion and without, I believe, reading each section of the bill. It might be claimed that the bill had been discussed in committee, but I have noticed that this time, as in several other instances, a group which, notwithstanding the small number of its members, represents a large section of the population, has been completely ignored and no member of my group was invited to sit on the committee appointed to examine this bill.
I do not propose to take up the time of the house, but I wish to protest against the discrimination shown to certain classes of soldiers.
Thus I find that the members of the reserve army will not have the right to vote unless they have reached the age of twenty-one, whereas the members of the active army will be entitled to vote if they are British subjects even though they are only eighteen or nineteen years old. I am glad that the right to vote has been granted to all those who are serving in the army, regardless of their age.
Besides, in connection with the debate on the plebiscite, I had moved an amendment to grant the right to vote to persons eighteen years of age, but the amendment was rejected by the house. Why bar the members of the reserve army, who are only eighteen and nineteen years of age, from voting, when they are being called up for military service? Why prevent them from voting when they are being mobilized at eighteen, under a hypocritical legislation, which has been called mobilization act while it is a conscription act, and when they are liable, as the minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), stated, to be called up for service overseas; indeed, they have been sent to Kiska, Jamaica and Newfoundland. This group of enlisted men are discriminated against and I wish to register my protest before this bill is passed.
Another unfair stipulation is that referring to the appointment of scrutineers. It states that "two of such scrutineers shall be nominated by the Leader of the Government, two by the Leader of the Opposition and two on the joint recommendation of the Leaders of political groups having a recognized membership in the House of Commons of eight or more." I lead a group which, as I stated a moment ago, has not a large membership in this house, but represents a large proportion of the people of this country. A proof of this statement is the fact that, last August, when two by-elections were held in the province of Quebec, the government candidates were badly defeated by representatives of the group of which I am a member.
One of our candidates was elected, and if the other was not successful it was because of the manipulation of lists. In spite of the representations we made to the Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty)-and I must say, by the way, that he is usually most courteous- he did not heed our protests under the circumstances. The lists were prepared in such a way that the names of quite a number of voters from the constituency of Montreal-Cartier were left out. We asked for representatives of our own, but our request was denied under the ' pretext that it had come too late. However, the candidate of the labour-progressive party, which had no member in this house, was allowed to have some
Dominion Elections Act

one watch the preparation of lists on his behalf. I am quite glad that such a privilege was granted to him, but why should not-I would not say the same privilege-but the same right, have been granted to a much more considerable group which has members in this house, a group that expresses the views of a large proportion of the Canadian people? It was claimed that our request was belated; well, I have here some documents and telegrams, showing that some kind of revision was ordered but that a sufficient number of officials could not be found, and they were denied to us so that the revision was a eomedy; thus hundreds of thousands of names were left out of the lists for the special purpose of preventing the election of the candidate representing the group which I have the honour to lead in this house. The same thing will happen again.
Something similar did happen in connection with the proposed revision of the standing orders of the House of Commons. A change was recommended whereby no division could be recorded unless requested by twenty members, instead of five as at present. The purpose of that change was to prevent a minority which represents a very large body of opinion to demand a vote on certain occasions. In the next general election, we shall have a very large number of candidates in the field, and we are not even going to have the right to have some one look after our interests. What happened in Montreal-Cartier in the 1917 election during the Great War, shows the extreme importance, if we are to have a political party, of having such a representative.
It is said in the bill that a person may "act as representative of a political party at the taking of such votes". But what is meant by a political party? Obviously, an endeavour will be made to interpret the expression "political party" in the light of another section which says that a party must, in order to enjoy that right, have at least eight members in the House of Commons. But a political party which has less than eight members in the house may have in the field, in the next election, more than one hundred candidates and that party will not have a single representative to look after its interests. Such is the discrimination made under this bill. Consequently before its third reading, I wish to voice my protest once more. Since it is claimed that we are fighting for freedom and the protection of the rights of minorities, I say that those minorities should be given the rights for which they are called upon to fight elsewhere.

Motion agreed to and bill read the third time.
Mr. ILSLEY moved that the bill do now pass and that the title be as on the order paper.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on two previous occasions I have given my reasons for opposing the making of gifts to England,, and I should like to put myself on record once more as being against this bill which provides for a gift of $800,000,000 to the united nations. Apparently the government intends to keep on enforcing measures such as this one despite the fact that the people of this country are opposing its stupid policy and are giving warning of their opposition. In the by-elections which were held last summer the people of this country condemned the enforcement of such a policy, but the government does not seem to want to listen to them at all.
It may be that if the results of the Saskatchewan provincial election were known certain people would open their ears and listen to these warnings. Only last summer when a provincial election was held in Ontario the two old parties were nearly wiped off the map. This indicates that the criticism and discontent of the people are coming not only from the province of Quebec but from all over Canada. If the government does not change its policy pretty soon, ultimately we shall have that socialism which makes everyone so frightened. I shall not make any further comments except to say that I strongly oppose this gift to the united nations.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker I have no intention of delaying for any time the consideration of this bill which has been moved for second reading by the Minister of Finance. On previous occasions I have expressed my personal views as to this method of assistance to people who in my opinion enjoy a better financial position than the people of Canada.

Mutual Aid
I do not need to advance any reasons additional to those I have previously expressed in opposition to a similar measure. I only want to repeat that it seems strange, to my humble judgment, that a small country like Canada, with a population of a little over eleven million, should be called upon to make a contribution or a gift-the name does not matter; the name was changed by the last legislation on this subject but it does not affect the principle at all-of one billion dollars last year and now eight hundred million dollars to a country which is many, many times richer than Canada is or will be for many generations to come. Let us not forget the facts to be considered in these circumstances.
The British empire, which has been directed for many years by highly gifted and talented diplomats and financiers, has developed to a point where it has become one of the greatest empires the world has ever known. Canada is a small country compared with the British empire. Canada is a very small country compared with the British isles. The people of Britain control directly or indirectly almost one-half of the civilized world, and they are in control financially speaking, commercially speaking, economically speaking, of over one-half of the population of the world. Canada is making a gift to that rich country, which for a long time has been the money market of the world, and which has not yet decided to abandon it.
We were told a few days ago, if not yesterday, that the British empire, or England, had been buying for cash to a larger amount than is represented by the gift that we have made in the past and the gift we propose to make under this bill. Is that not an indication that that great country is quite capable of taking care of her obligations and that there is no necessity for a small country like Canada, not a member of the Big Four, to be called upon to make a contribution of $800,000,000? It is said, it is true, that that money goes to other countries as well, but if one looks at the report that has been made by the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), it will be ascertained that the British empire received of our gift last year three-quarters of a billion dollars. They are capable, financially speaking and economically speaking, of paying, if not at present, at least later, for the purchases they are making in Canada. Why should we be called upon to make such a gift now?
Let us not forget, Mr. Speaker, that at present the cost of the war to the Canadian people is as high as the burden it has imposed upon any of the allied nations of today. The daily cost of the war has risen,
according to a recent government publication, "Canada at War", from three cents per head of the population of Canada to $1.16 per head in 1943. That means about $425 a year for every man, woman and child in Canada today. The burden is heavy enough, and I do not think we should be called upon to make an additional contribution in this form.
Far from my mind is the idea that we should not supply what the allied nations need to carry on the war. We should continue to supply the materials they require, the armaments and the food that we have been supplying up to the present time. But why not at least keep a record of it in our books as an advance made to a country which is ten times, a hundred times, richer than Canada? Why not have an open account in order that when the war is over, when all the difficulties and consequences of the war are to be settled, when advantages are to be divided amongst the nations, Canada will have on the ledger something to offset claims that might be made against her or to justify any claim that Canada might see fit to make when the settlement of debts is being made. What harm would it be for Canada to keep a ledger account showing the advances we are making to Britain, if she is not at present in a position to pay in cash for the goods we are sending her? What objection could there be to having that recorded in a ledger in order that we shall have a clear account of our disbursements for the day of final settlement?
An argument has been made which to my mind has no value. It is said: What is the use of having debts on the books that will never be paid? Mr. Speaker, is it not a reflection on the credit of British institutions and on the credit of Britain to say that she will never be in a position to pay for the materials and goods she needs at present and that we have to make her a gift in order to prevent Britain from finding herself later on in the humiliating position of not being able to pay the price of the goods we have sent her? I think that argument is of no value at all. Suppose the debt is not going to be paid, as is argued. There is no objection to keeping an account of that debt in order that we may be able to show after the war is over what Canada has really done in this war, what her contribution to the war has been. It will be interesting then to have that figure, showing the amount we have advanced to the British empire in order to help the British empire to carry on a war that has been started, we will say, for the sake of saving the liberty of the world.
Mutual Aid

It has been argued, on the other hand, that we should remember that by making these supplies available to the British empire we are providing our workmen with work through the manufacture of the weapons of war and providing our agriculturists with work in supplying foodstuffs. That is a poor argument in my judgment, a very poor argument, Mr. Speaker. If we have that amount of money to spend on manufacturing materials of war and procuring foodstuffs to be given away in the form of gifts, we could very well use that money and that power of production to produce things which are needed in this country and could be consumed here. We could spend this money on articles which would be useful to Canadians, not merely to make goods on the pretext that the purpose is to provide business for our manufacturers and our industrial and agricultural producers. These arguments, in my humble judgment, are no good, and I contend there is no justification in the world for the attitude we have been taking, and are taking at the present time. Without desiring to be unfair or to use unduly severe language, as I was accused of doing last year when I advanced this argument, I would repeat that this is a colonial tribute. Last year it was argued that there was no tribute because our act was voluntary. Well, even if the payment is voluntary, even if these goods are voluntarily given, none the less it is a tribute which we are paying to a country or to a people far richer at this time, and likely to remain so for long after the war is over, than is Canada herself.
The example of the United States may be cited. We may be told that the United States have had for a long time a similar measure on their statute books and that they have been acting under that measure. Surely nobody will seriously make a comparison between Canada and the United States; nobody will compare our wealth, our power of production or our facilities for production with those of the United States. There is no comparison possible either in the economic field, in the matter of population, or in the field of external authority or international authority.
hether we like it or not, we have to recognize that our status sis a country cannot be compared internationally with the status of the United States. The United States is an independent country. I know that some hon. members and some newspaper men will say: Well, is not Canada an independent country? I have no hesitation in saying: No, she is not an independent country. This fact was established with the full approval of the government, when the late Minister of Justice argued in this house that Canada could not

be neutral in this war, that Canada had to go into the war the moment that one part of the British commonwealth was in the war. I conclude from that argument that we are not an independent country. I agree that we went into this war voluntarily, and I am not ashamed of the action I took at that time. But we went into the war because Britain was at war. Justification can be found for this statement even in the recent speeches made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in London and here in this House of Commons. We went into the war because we were a member of the British commonwealth of nations. This is a society or group of nations, each of which is committed to the defence of the interests of the others; otherwise there could be no such society of nations; there could be ho commonwealth without a responsibility on the part of one of the members of the commonwealth toward the interests of any other member which might be endangered. We are not an independent country. We may, if we choose, make a subtle argument on points of law, on texts of jurisprudence and on statutes, but in reality and in practice we have never acted as an independent country, and from the point of view of responsibility and action we are not independent, far less a sovereign nation capable of disposing of herself.
So that we are not in the same position as the United States. Further, the United States have another reason for having entered into the war as they did, two years after Canada declared war. They were attacked. They are on the defensive. They had been assailed by Japan and they are fighting in this war because, having been attacked by that powerful empire, they have a much greater interest in the war than Canada has.
Our position therefore is not at all comparable with that in which the United States find themselves, and we should not be expected to do everything that has been done in that country with regard to this war. We are doing a mighty effort. Canada deserves the credit and praise of all the nations of the world for what she has been doing, because in reality she is doing more than she was ever expected to do in a conflict like this one. After all, this war, according to an Englishspeaking writer, is a war first of all for power, with liberty and freedom as a result of obtaining power. One has only to go into the library of parliament to find several books by Englishspeaking writers, Canadians and others, indicating that this war is a war for power. I do not object to that. We have to fight force with force. But I contend that Canada has been

Mutual Aid
doing a lot more than she was expected to do, a lot more than it was thought she would be capable of doing.
We are not among the Big Four. What is the use of our boasting and making all the propaganda which is being issued? We are not going to be consulted when the peace terms are drafted; we shall be informed what the decision has been after the four great powers have met, and Canada will have to accept their decisions and the consequences. With that I find no fault, Canada is not one of the great powers of the world. We are a small nation with great aspirations and with very strong hopes for the future, but we have not yet realized our hopes; we have not yet achieved what we think we are capable of achieving by the development of all our resources. We are still a small nation of eleven millions and we should not load ourselves with too many debts, because we do not know what the situation is going to be when peace does come.
I repeat, I am not objecting so much to the fact that we are spending money in the manufacture of armaments and the production of food in order to help the allies, but I want a statement to be kept of what we are giving to the British empire so that when the time does come to divide what there is to be divided, if there is anything to be divided, something will be there to represent in totality what is the share of Canada.
These are my views, which I have expressed as calmly as I could and in all sincerity, though without much hope of making any change in the minds of the hon. members sitting in this house. They are entitled to their own views, their own opinions, as I am entitled to mine. They are as free as I am to express their views openly and to voice their sentiments; otherwise what are we fighting for, if not for the liberty to express our opinions, whether it pleases or not the majority or the minority in Canada? I am under no misapprehension as to the effect of my observations. I feel that they will not convince the supporters of the government; they will not convince the members of the opposition and other members in the house; they will not even shake the conviction of a large section of the representatives of the province of Quebec in this House of Commons. Those members will continue just the same to support the government in this measure, as they have supported the government on other measures. But I thought that I should again speak openly on the subject. This question to my mind is one of the important matters we have to deal with in debating matters relating to the war.
I have the satisfaction at least of having voiced the views and the thoughts of the majority of the citizens of my province. I will go farther than that and say that they are also the views and the thoughts of many citizens living in other provinces.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. H. KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre):
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
The views of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation on this important measure have been expressed on previous occasions when comparable bills were before the house, so that it is not necessary for me to speak at any considerable length. However,
I feel that our position should be restated. First of all, we accept the indivisibility of the common cause in which we are all engaged at the present time. Acting from that premise, we agree with those who feel that we should make to the fullest of our capacity whatever contribution we can, whether it be in service on our own behalf or whether it be a contribution to our allies over and above what they purchase from us, as is proposed in this bill.
I know that the government, perhaps I should say members of the party on the opposite side, do not often give us credit for some of the things we do; but I think this should be said, that we in this group, despite the fact that in some quarters there is misunderstanding of this measure, despite the fact that there is some criticism of it, definitely avoid making any political capital out of that criticism. In fact we go to the other extreme and do our best to set aside misunderstanding and to explain just what this bill involves. I know that efforts along that line have been made in particular by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), who leads this group, and I would hope that further efforts might be made by a number of parties in this house, and that still further efforts might be made by the government to allay the misunderstandings that exist in certain quarters. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has done a pretty good job along that line in some of the statements that he has made in this house. I would suggest to the government that through its propaganda agencies of one sort or another, this is a job that should be undertaken throughout the country, to help our people realize that what we have in this measure is not some mark of colonial subjugation, not some means of bankrupting the country, but rather a means whereby we are enabled to make a contribution of which I feel Canadians generally are proud.
I repeat that, as we see it, this bill-the whole concept of mutual aid legislation-is based on the principle of the absolute indivisibility of the struggle in which we are

Mutual Aid

engaged. I may say at this point that we feel that that principle should be kept in mind for the years that lie ahead. Never again, I hope, shall we think of the world in which we live as one which can be divided up into small sectors. We are engaged in this war as one set of united nations. When the struggle is over, if we are to have peace, it too must be recognized as indivisible, and some of the principles we are seeking to carry out in this bill, such as those involved in UNRRA, we feel, must be carried over and extended in the post-war period.
It warms my heart to talk at times with members of this house from other parties and to find how general, how sincere, how earnest is the desire of members, whatever their political or social philosophy may be, that we may not have to go into another world war some years after this one is over. I earnestly plead that we should recognize, as one principle upon which we must act if we are to avoid another war, the indivisibility of peace and the necessity of being concerned about the lot of our brothers the world over. I hope we shall never forget the principle upon which we have acted in passing these mutual aid bills from year to year.
Another principle which I feel is highlighted by the passing of this bill was stated particularly well by the Minister of Finance on March 3, 1943, at page 931 of Hansard. I should like to quote a sentence which I feel is very significant:
No country goes bankrupt in this way;-
And I emphasize the remainder of the sentence:
-no country goes bankrupt by increasing its production and devoting part or all or more than all of that increase to a supreme cause.
The minister was answering arguments advanced by certain opposition members to the effect that the country was being bankrupted by the huge sums of money being spent on the war. He made certain other comments at that time as well, which I feel might be quoted again, though I do not wish anyone to think I agree with everything said by the Minister of Finance because I am giving these quotations. I quote now from page 930 of Hansard for last year:
We do not pay for the war out of some hoard of money that we have accumulated in the past. ye pay for it out of the taxes and savings that we obtain from the current income of the whole nation. We shall not run short of money.
I emphasize that; the minister said, "We shall not run short of money."
Indeed, our danger is the very reverse of that, namely, that we may pile up too much money in -the pockets and bank accounts of 
Canadians, unless w'e strive with every effort to promote the sale of victory bonds and war savings certificates.
If we are bankrupting the nation, is it not indeed a strange type of -bankruptcy? How can we use such a term to describe the process under which this country has doubled its national income in three years, has wiped out unemployment, has multiplied its production of many things and learned many types of newr skills, has expanded and diversified its production equipment, has multiplied its governmental revenues by more than four times, has enabled millions of its citizens to acquire a nest-egg for the future, has mobilized its -full strength as a producing machine, -and has developed a sense of productive achievement not hitherto known ?
Immediately following that the minister used the words I have quoted already. It seems to me that at that time he laid down a principle which underlies mutual aid, which underlies the mobilizing and organizing of our productive capacity for the war effort, and which should stand before us as a principle to be carried into the post-war period. Many of us are criticized, and some hon. members attempt in their criticism to make us appear ridiculous, when we advocate a much higher standard of living for the Canadian people after the war, when we suggest what at present seem rather high figures for old age pensions, and matters of the kind; yet on that same day the Minister of Finance said:
We can and must make use of that increased capacity after the war. We must develop that potential to the maximum. If we do, we can develop a far higher standard of living for the average Canadian than 'he has ever known before. . . .
My point is that I believe the Minister of Finance is absolutely right when he says we do not bankrupt a country by tremendously increasing our productive capacity and devoting a huge portion of that increase, or more than the increase, to a great cause. That is what we are doing at the present time, and that is what many of us hope we will do after the war. We maintain that we are not advocating something ridiculous, that we are not advocating bankruptcy when we say that following the war the economy of this country should be organized on a basis of full, all-out production to meet a great cause then, just as we are called upon to meet a great cause now. At the present time the great cause is the defeat of nazism and the preservation of our liberties. When the war is over the great cause will be the demands of peace, of a better life for all our people. I am sure the hon. members who preceded me-will agree that this principle should be acted upon in the post-war period, and I had -hoped that perchance this year they might have reached the point where they would have some hope-

Mutual Aid
that this would be done-that after the war we would continue the policy of organizing our production on a high level and devoting a large portion of it to the great cause of peace. My hope was that some of those who have opposed these measures previously might come to understand them in those terms and be prepared to support the measure this year, realizing that the struggle in which we are engaged is a great task, and having the hope and assurance that the same principle would be carried over into the post-war period; for that is our position.
During the past several days references have been made on a number of occasions to getting certain things free. I feel that the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) perhaps chose the wrong word when he spoke of getting things for nothing, even with respect to mutual aid, for example. Nothing in this world is had for nothing. The world is not getting free the supplies that we make available. We in Canada, as part of the united nations, are contributing the effort, the energy and the work necessary to produce those supplies. But what is involved, if I -may again use the language of the Minister of Finance, is this: that on a national scale, indeed on a united nations scale, we are planning for the greatest production possible. Then, by a national decision, we take a portion of that great production and devote it to a great cause. What we are asking in the post-war period, when we suggest there should be better old age pensions and other forms of social security and a higher standard of living for our people, is not that something be given for nothing, not that something be plucked out of thin air, but that this same principle be carried over; that we organize our production on a national scale on the highest possible basis, and then, by a national decision, take a large portion of that increased production and devote it to a great cause.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I made some comments on this matter yesterday when it was in the resolution stage. There is not a great deal more that I care to say, but since the bill is up for second reading and some hon. members have

Mutual Aid
preceded me, I am prompted to say a few things further. This group was in favour of the principle embodied in this bill as far back as when we first began to give aid to Britain a few years ago, and has consistently favoured it throughout.
On the surface the bill appears to be a magnanimous gesture on the part of Canada toward the united nations, but it may not be so magnanimous when all the details of the intricate financial operations are understood.
I do not claim to understand them all. On the surface it appears that we are producing so much goods and are taking $800,000,000 worth of them and giving them to the united nations. That is the general and broad principle ; that is why it appears to be a magnanimous gesture. When it comes to the financial operations and all the details of how the thing is handled, that is another matter, and one which requires a good deal of study. I do not claim to be a financial expert. As a matter of fact some of us have been studying some of these things for a good many years and even now I must confess that I feel I am only beginning to. touch the fringe of a tremendous and vast subject. That is the thought that strikes me when I begin to go into all the intricacies of the machinery of our financial operations.
However, it does not take a great deal of study or a superabundance of intelligence to understand a few of the outstanding principles embodied in a measure of this kind or even in the general economy of the country or of nations as a whole. I said that on the face of it this bill appears to be a magnanimous gesture to the united nations, and I do not see how one can oppose it on those grounds. I have heard the remarks of one or two speakers this afternoon and it seems to me they might benefit from an imaginative illustration of what the government is doing. Let us suppose I find myself mixed up in a sort of brawl, that I am faced with a parade of rebels coming down the street with torches, sticks, guns, axes and clubs and my neighbours come running to me saying: They are going to burn down your house; they are against us! My friends step out and try to disperse the mob, and in doing so they use my axe, my gun and my pitchfork. After they have dispersed the mob should I turn to them and say: Thank you, gentlemen; that was a wonderful thing, . but you have destroyed my axe, you have broken my pitchfork, and I will have to charge you for them; you have destroyed my land and my garden, and you must pay me so much money?
Of course you would say that would be a foolish thing to do; you would say it would be senseless to do that. But in principle that
is exactly what is happening. I am certain that if it had not been for many circumstances the nazis might have completed their march of the continents. Some things have happened in this war which were considered impossible when it started. When we see that happening which was thought to be impossible, there is no reason to sit back and say: We are far away from the scene; the nazis can never get over here. They might have got over here; we do not know.
For instance, what happened to Great Britain? That country took the greatest possible punishment that any nation could take. The hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Jaques) was in England a few months ago, and he told me the other day that one out of ten people you see on the streets of England is in uniform. We know that England took it. What are we doing now? We are simply saying: We want to share in this; and we take measures such as this to carry out that wish.
However, as I said, it may not be such a wonderful thing when we consider the details of its operation. The minister may correct me if my diagnosis of these operations is not the right one. There are a lot of intricacies about the way this proposal operates. I cannot go into the minister's department and discover this, that or the other thing, although I might be welcomed there. It seems to me that the net result of all this kind of legislation is simply that we are giving Great Britain a credit of $800,000,000. That is reflected in the goods that we ship over there.
I do not know whether the minister will answer this at some future time, but I should like to ask whether it makes any material difference, whether $800,000,000 will go into the Canadian debt structure or $800,000,000 into the British debt structure. The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) said, as I understood him, that he wanted to know the goods that went over there, that there should be a sort of inventory made of what was shipped out. To my mind in an operation of this kind it does not make a particle of difference what is shipped out. As a matter of fact I have some doubt whether the government can tell us what goods will actually come under this particular measure. So far as I can see, in the end it only means that Great Britain will not have to pay Canada $800,000,000. In other words, $800,000,000 is lopped off Great Britain's debt to Canada.
There is another aspect of the matter which, while it has not confused me, has given me occasion for some little thought. While this may appear to be a gift to Britain, in reality it is not a gift of goods to the Briitsh people.
Mutual Aid

In other words, the British people are not getting their goods for nothing. They have to pay for them just the same. A million sacks of flour, we will say, go over to Great Britain. Suppose there is a label on those sacks of flour, "Gift to Britain" or "Mutual Aid to Britain-milled in Canada." That does not mean for a moment that the people of Britain can go to the retail stores and say: Oh, this is a gift to us; I will take one of those sacks of flour. No, the people of Great Britain when they want to buy that flour must pay, to use the expression of the Minister of Finance, cash on the barrel head, whatever that may be-I do not know why barrel head is brought into it. I would like the minister or some other competent authority to trace that money through. Here are half a million people buying half a million dollars' worth of our goods. The money comes out of their pockets. It passes over the counters. The retailers get the money and pay their debts, and where does the money eventually repose? I ask that question. I have not been able to follow it through. Does it repose in the British treasury, or does it repose in some purchasing board or in the banking institutions of Great Britain? That may be a small matter, but it is something I would like to have made clear. So far as I can see, the only result is that 8800,000,000 of credit is cut off from the debt owed by Great Britain to Canada.
May I put it in this way? We pass this bill, and we send to Great Britain 8800,000,000 worth of goods. Those goods have to be paid for in Canada; the 8800,000,000 to pay for them comes out of either borrowings or taxation, and I think it will be discovered that most of it comes out of borrowings. The people of Canada then owe the greater portion of that 8800,000,000; for it is chalked up as part of the national debt. Personally I do not believe that Canada's debt will ever be paid off; it may be, but I do not think so.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext: Not with this government.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I do not think it will be paid off with any government, and when I make that statement let me say emphatically that I am not breaking down any confidence which the people of Canada have in the victory bonds they now hold. They will be paid, certainly. They will be paid through some sort of refunding scheme; we shall continue to refund every so many years and the debt will still remain. This 8800,000,000 will go into our debt structure, and it can remain there, so far as I am concerned, for centuries to come. The burden on the people of Canada is to pay the interest on that
8800,000,000.

Let us transplant our thoughts for a moment to Great Britain. Suppose Great Britain handles her debt as we handle ours, and retires her maturing obligations only by postponing them through a process of refunding. If my premise is right, why cannot the $800,000,000 go into the debt structure of Britain instead of into ours?	That is a
question I should like to have answered if possible.
Some who have spoken this afternoon have referred to the merits of this bill with respect to the post-war period. By this bill a certain principle is established, I agree; and what is the principle? The principle that is established is that it is possible to pay for something, and then after you have paid for it or borrowed to pay for it-I do not care how it is done-it is possible to give it away.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has stated that what we need in the post-war period is to organize our production on a very high level, perhaps on a higher level than that of to-day. I have no fault to find with that, except that if that is all you do, you do not solve the problem; for the problem that Canada faces now is not the problem of production at all. That problem has been solved. As the Minister of Munitions and Supply said last night, our present productive genius has reached the point where we can produce everything in Canada. The problem now is how to get the goods to the people. You cannot get them to the people through the amount of money that goes into the pockets of the people in wages, salaries, dividends, interest and profits, because there is not enough money coming out of that process to buy back all the goods that can be produced, and so you will always have a surplus of goods. As the surpluses pile up, you are going to put men out of work. The problem is not to find everybody jobs. As a matter of fact in a very high order of civilization the cutting down of the working hours, reducing the number of man-hours, giving people more time to themselves-that is the ideal objective. If by a process of using purchasing power as a free gift to our people, starting with old age pensions if you like, you can buy the surplus goods and get them into the hands of the people who need them, I ask, is there anything wrong with that? Oh, somebody may say, that would be something for nothing. My friend says it does not come out of thin air. Let me change the terminology and say that by the use of free purchasing power the money will come out of the end of a fountain pen; for that is the way the money comes out now, and it stands as a debt.

Mutual Aid
If the principle of this bill is right-and evidently it is, for it is working-there is no reason why the principle of the bill cannot be applied in the post-war period. There is no reason why we cannot produce and buy the goods, do the same thing we are doing under this bill, but give them to our .own people instead of to the people of other nations. That is my position.
I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that an important principle is involved here, and the charming thing about it is that it is a principle that is working. Let us put it to work inside Canada when peace comes.
We in this group, Mr. Speaker, are in favour of the bill.
Mr. KARL K. HOMUTH (Waterloo South): Before we carry this bill there are one or two remarks I would like to make with respect to it. I listened attentively to the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), acting leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, this afternoon, and his enunciation of great principles touching what we should do and where Canada should stand. My memory went back to the years 1938, 1939 and 1940, when the principle enunciated by the hon. member's party was that the only attitude Canada should take in the war was, how much profit could we make out of it and how many jobs could be provided in this country by supplying materials for overseas.
The one matter about which I am alarmed is as to what materials are being purchased with the money voted under this and like bills. No one doubts that, regardless of all the resolutions which are passed and all the committees which are set up, when the war is over there will be strong economic competition between countries. In the little yellow book containing the report of the Canadian mutual aid board I note a list, running only to the end of March, 1944, of of some of the things we are purchasing and providing for Russia. That country has always been represented to Canadians by members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party as a land flowing with milk and honey, with an ideal diversity and divisibility of effort, where nothing is wrong, where collective farming and every other activity ordinarily associated with socialism is practised; and in this list I observe that large numbers of machines and quantities of other equipment are being dispatched to Russia under this mutual aid arrangement. If my information is correct, orders from Soviet Russia to the value of millions upon millions of dollars are now being worked on in various factories
of the dominion. I think the people of Canada would like to know whether these products, particularly these machines, are for war purposes. Personally I think they are not, because the orders I have in mind cannot be completed before the end of the war if the war 'should end within the next two or three years. How much of the money allocated to mutual aid is going in payment of these machines? It must be assumed that these machines are to go into the economic set-up of Soviet Russia and will be operating in the economic war which will follow this war; and unless the Russians raise their standards of living to those of Canada-which, however some may criticize them, are the highest of any country in the world-these machines will be operated against the interests of the working men of Canada.
Mr. II.SLEY:	The hon. gentleman is mistaken. No non-war machines are being supplied to Soviet Russia on mutual aid.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I am willing to take the
minister's word for that, but it does not wholly reassure me. If Russia has money to pay for these millions upon millions of dollars' worth of orders which are being given in Canada for the advantage of their future economy, they should be able to pay for some of the things which come under the mutual aid scheme. I do not know how the matter is worked out. I doubt if the minister knows; I doubt whether anyone knows except Russia herself. It is a serious matter, and we should see to it that whatever money we freely give or whatever equipment is provided without charge is given in such a way that the interests of Canadian working men will not be .jeopardized when the war is over.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I not only support the administration in the $800 million mutual aid bill, but, as the minister probably knows, I go somewhat farther. I did not have the pleasure this afternoon of hearing the remarks of the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) or all the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles); but knowing the tenor of the remarks of the first-mentioned hon. member I should like to say a few things with regard to what I consider mutual aid to be.
The present resolution calls for an additional $800 million, which is $200 million less than last year. As to the part of the $800 million *which goes to Britain, we know that Great Britain has virtually no Canadian assets with which to pay for the war material which she receives.
Mutual Aid

penses. The amount of $2,800,000,000 which we have spent in the past three years represents a debt of $250 per capita upon Canada's 11,600,000 inhabitants.
Apart from Canada, only the United States has given mutual aid, but the wealth and income of that country are far greater than our own. Their present national income amounts to the tremendous sum of $180,000,000,000 per annum, which is about twenty times higher than ours, and their revenue for 1944 will come to $42,578,000,000, that is, about twenty times our figure. According to a preliminary report submitted by the Lend-Lease Board and put on record in the American senate last April, the United States between March 31, 1941, when they adopted the lend-lease bill, and March 31, 1944, delivered, under lend-lease, various goods amounting to $21,794,000,000.
That represents, mind you, only 5 per cent of their national income for the last three years, whereas our gifts equal 12 per cent: that also is only 25 per cent of their federr' income for the same period, as compared with 37 per cent in the case of Canada; in fact, that represents an increase of only 15 per cent in their public debt since 1942, as compared with 50 per cent in the case of Canada. On -the other hand, we have had nothing in return, absolutely nothing. Yet, our war effort is greater than that of any other country; we are making gifts which no other country makes. Here is what the United States receive for the mutual aid it gives in the form of lease-lend loans. It has obtained naval and air bases in British colonies on this side of the Atlantic and industrial and commercial advantages in latin America, Africa and the Far East; for instance, in Australia, lease-lend assistance serves to pay the cost of the maintenance of American troops in the Pacific zone, which reduces to that extent the apparent amount provided in the form of mutual aid. Until now, Canada has not benefited from mutual aid, or at least the government have never disclosed anything in that connection.
Now, is any thought being given to what these sums represent for Canada; is it realized which use this country could have made of the 82,800.000,000 it has distributed outright?
In the first place, a better salary could have been paid to our workers. According to the Marsh report, in 1941 the annual income of about 62 per cent of Canadian wage-earners was under $950; yet, a gift of one billion dollars was made! At this time the annual income of nearly 60 per cent of Canadian 
wage-earners is lower than $1,400 which is the minimum on which a family may enjoy a decent standard of living.
To what other uses could that money have been put? It could have helped to raise the public health standard. The medical examination of draftees shows that about 55 per cent, of these men are unfit for active service. Those gifts could have been used for the elimination of slums in our larger cities. Let it be remembered that to-day in the city of Montreal some families have to live in garages. People were living in shacks where children suffered from cold last winter under conditions that are absolutely unsanitary and where those children are exposed to tuberculosis. That is what could have, but has not, been done. It was deemed preferable to achieve a war effort greater than that of any other country, and to make further gifts, amounting to billions of dollars.
Mr. Chairman, those are some of the reasons why I oppose this new gift of $800,000,000.
(Text):
i Mr. NORMAN JAQUES (Wetaskiwin): Mr. Speaker, since it was my good fortune to spend several months last winter in Great Britain I feel I should pay a humble tribute to the people of that country for the contribution, they have made and are making to, the common cause of winning the war. Mention has been made of Canada's gift to Great Britain and the allied cause, but may I remind some hon. members that those gifts had to be taken by sea and distributed to the various countries. I travelled to Great Britain in a convoy last December and I was two weeks on the Atlantic after leaving Halifax. I talked to the officers and men of the ship I was on, and I learned a lot and heard a lot about the business of convoying which I had not heard before and which I doubt very much the majority of people know to-day.
Unlike battles on the land or naval engagements, the convoys are more or less secret. Losses are not reported. I was unpleasantly surprised to hear that at the time I was crossing sinkings were quite frequent. I do not think there was a man on the ship, and if there was I did not meet him, who had not been torpedoed at least once. The captain had had three ships sunk under him and most of the officers and the crew had experienced more than one sinking. I must confess that I found those two weeks rather trying, not knowing from one minute to the other whether the ship might be suddenly blown up. Mine was a voyage of only two weeks, but the merchant seamen of Great Britain have been undergoing this strain since the beginning of the war nearly five years ago and will continue-

Mutual Aid
to undergo it until the end of the war. I do not think any words of mine are capable of conveying the debt that we owe these men.
I should like to say one word about the convoys to Russia. I was told by some of the officers who had been on Russian convoys that losses of thirty per cent were not uncommon and that on one occasion every ship in the convoy was destroyed. The situation became so bad that for a time that route was discontinued and supplies were sent around the cape of Good Hope and through the near east to Russia.
The people of Great Britain are contributing by means of a reduced standard of living. The ship I was on carried 4,000 tons of Canadian bacon. When I got to Bristol I went into a refreshment room in the station and I suppose the Canadian bacon suggested a ham sandwich to me. I asked the girl at the counter for a ham sandwich and she looked at me and said,
" What did you say?" I said, " I just want a ham sandwich." She said, " Here are the sandwiches." I said, "What are they?" She said, " Paste." I said, " What do you mean by paste?" She said, " God knows, it is coloured and flavoured; that is all I can tell you." I do not think she was far wrong.
In all the weeks that I spent in Great Britain I never saw a piece of beef, let alone taste it. Beef was not for the civilian. I was in some of the best clubs in London and the best they could provide was some curried rabbit. There was no beef or steak, none of the things we are accustomed to here. Even the glass of sherry had become unprocurable. [DOT] I had some wine that came from Algiers, but I was advised to put salt in it which might improve the flavour.
Then Great Britain has had her air raids. I saw several air raids and I saw the evidence of former raids in a number of the cities, such as London, Southampton, Bristol, Liverpool and one or two smaller places. In Southampton, for instance, the whole of the central part of the city has gone. It is as though in Ottawa all of Sparks street and Bank street had disappeared. I was told that the situation in other cities was worse, even for instance, in Plymouth, Hull and Coventry. It was bad enough in the cities that I saw.
Then there is the blackout, which we are spared but which they have to endure. The blackout by itself is bad enough, but when you add fog to it you have a situation that is positively alarming. I was caught one night in the blackout and a London fog. I thought I knew what a London fog meant because I had seen plenty of them before I came to Canada. But I had never seen fog combined with the blackout. There I was in the very
centre of London, at six o'clock in the evening, with not a light visible, not a sound to be heard. I was going from the Overseas club in Dean's yard, Westminster, to Victoria station and the only way I could get along was by tapping my stick along the edge of the pavement. I passed a convoy of about eight buses crawling behind a man carrying an oil flare, getting home the best way they could. The people of Britain have had to put up with those conditions for years, which we in Canada fortunately have been spared.
Travelling by train is another hardship. The trains are terribly overcrowded. I remember going from London to Scotland between Christmas and New Year's. I took the precaution to take a first-class ticket and I was in the station an hour and a half before the train started, but that did not help me very much. I should have known better but I had been asked to go and I could not very well refuse. I was caught between two armies at King's Cross. One army was returning to Scotland from Christmas leave and the other army was going to Scotland to celebrate New Year's. I was in between the two armies. The railway officials just threw up their hands and left us to it. I stood there for an hour and a half before the train came in, and I was very lucky to be able to get on board, let alone get a seat. The windows of the train could not be opened because of the blackout; in a very short time the air became difficult to breathe, and I wondered if I was going to survive. I knew I could not stand the whole twelve hours to Edinburgh and I said to myself, "Eventually, so why not now?" And I lay down on the floor and then realized that I had a carpet to lie on at least for the extra first-class fare.
Those are some of the things which, if you look at it in the right way, the people of Great Britain are contributing and have been contributing to the war effort. We have been spared these hardships and inconveniences. Our standard of living is practically as good as it was before the war. There is some inconvenience but not much. You can always with a little trouble get a berth on a train in Canada, but you cannot do so in Britain. You have to stand, and you are lucky if you can get on the train.
Finally, I should like to mention the battle of Britain. In my opinion and in the opinion of most people the war would be over had Britain gone down then. No aid would have been possible to our allies, no invasion of France, no bombing of Germany. Long before this the war would have been over for the greater part of the world. Whether the Germans could have extended their operations
Mutual Aid

to the western hemisphere I do not know, but there is no doubt about this, that had it not been for the sacrifices and the achievements of the Royal Air Force Britain would have gone down. With the R.A.F. and the R.C.A.F., of whom Churchill said, "Never was so much owed by so many to so few", I should like to link the Polish air force, which fought superbly in the battle of Britain. I was told over and over again that the Polish air force had played a very great part in winning the battle of Britain, that possibly they turned the scale. I was told that in skill and daring they were not surpassed even by our own air force. I mention that because I have not seen it in print and I think our debt to the Polish air force and to Poland should be acknowledged.
These are just a few remarks, Mr. Speaker, that I thought I should like to make as a personal tribute to the sacrifices which the people of Britain have been making ever since the war started and which I observed in the short time when I was over there. I felt that I should take this opportunity to pay that tribute.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our attitude toward this bill depends on one thing and one thing alone, namely, whether or not we regard this war as our war, as Canada's war, a war in which Canada as one of the allies must put forth its utmost effort. On that score the attitude of this house and of the people of Canada since the outbreak of the war leaves no room for doubt whatever. This is Canada's war, and that means, if we are honest with ourselves and regard our responsibilities seriously, that we must do everything we can to assist in winning the war. We have been fortunate in Canada. We have been spared a great deal of what other nations have suffered. We have been fortunate because of geography, because the United Kingdom stood betw'een us and our common enemy, because she had the spirit and the will to resist when the odds were terribly against her. We have also been spared in Canada because of our own contribution, and if we are sometimes told that that contribution made a crucial difference to Britain and the cause for which we are fighting, then we should be happy that we were in a position to make that contribution when we alone were in a position to make it. What we did with our aid to the United Kingdom and what we have done with our aid to the other allies fighting on our side was to put arms into the hands of those who could best use them for us as well as for ourselves, whether they were our soldiers or the soldiers of our allies and of the sister members of the commonwealth.
rMr. Jaques.]
The hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie (Mr. Raymond) suggested that we should get machine for machine and dollar for dollar. I would have thought that he would be one of those who would recognize that you cannot measure everything in material terms, that you cannot measure everything in terms of machines and dollars, that there are human and spiritual and moral values, and that we are not only fighting for those values but fighting with those values. We cannot match our contribution in terms of minerals, and metals and munitions and money with the contributions of other nations such as China, Russia and the United Kingdom, that have made such tremendous sacrifices in lives.
In fact that kind of argument leads to comparisons which not only have no validity but actually are definitely harmful to the cause of the united nations. The united nations depend for their success-and they have a long way to go-on their staying united, on their having trust in each other, on their sharing the burdens in proportion to their ability to bear those burdens. We shall not stay united if we begin to compare sacrifices in terms of so many men, so many lives, so many dollars, and try to strike that kind of impossible balance. All that we can do, if we recognize that this is our war, is to do our utmost in every direction.
It so happens that Canada is one of the few nations on the face of the earth which to-day have an exportable surplus of munitions of war. That is because of our natural resources, because of our geographical position, because of the wa3r in which farmers, industry, management and government have combined to make those resources available when they were needed to make the utmost contribution to the allied cause.
But also, Mr. Speaker, it is important in our discussions in the difficult days which lie ahead-they are going to be difficult-that we should not compare the contributions of different classes and groups in the community with those of other classes and groups, any more than we should make comparisons between the contributions of different nations. No one can measure the contribution of Britain in any measurable terms; no one can measure the contribution of Russia in measurable terms; and I suggest that that kind of comparison should be left out of our discussion if we are to stay united. But also we must stay united not only on the international front against the enemy, but, in order to make our utmost effort, we must stay united on the national front at home.
Consequently, I am sure that all hon. members deprecate comparisons between different

Mutual Aid
parts of the country and different classes. I am sorry in a way that I was drawn into making such a comparison, or followed someone who did, in the discussion on June 6, when the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) said that industry is just as vital to the war effort as what is being done by the soldiers. Well, it did not seem to me that that particular day, when our soldiers had just landed on the shores of Europe, was a good day to make that remark, and I denied its validity. I think I was right in doing that. But I recognize, of course, as do all hon, members, that it is only by the combined efforts of our farmers, our workers, our soldiers, of all our people, of all our organizations and governments, that we can make not only the effort of which we are capable in the war- and which has won the admiration of the world-but also the effort we should make to win the peace after the war.
Unity at home and unity abroad are two things we need to have above everything else. I most sincerely hope that hon. members and others outside will agree with me that comparisons, except for the purposes of decent emulation, are not only invidious but are likely to divide us and divide our allies and assist the enemy, whether that enemy be Hitler or Japan, or the enemies we shall have to meet after the war in the form of poverty and ill health and the other foes we shall then have to face.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), speaking in London, said:
Canada's fight for freedom will be a fight to the finish. It is clear to our people that this war is all one war: a monstrous conspiracy of the fascist powers to dominate and enslave the world. Having taken up arms of their own free wrill, the Canadian people will not relax until freedom is secure. Canada's effort will be an enduring effort.
We have also sought to look beyond the war; to make our effort a long-range effort. The Canadian people, no less than the people of Britain, whose sacrifices have been so great, need the promise of a brighter future. To sustain us in our endeavours, we all need the vision of a new world order.
By coordinated action, by mutual aid, by continuous cooperation, the united nations are achieving military victory. The widest measure of cooperation will be no less needed in the making and keeping of peace. While our primary aim, like yours, is military victory, our ultimate aim, like yours, is a better future for mankind.
This bill and the great purpose it aims to carry out are part of our work to win the war. It also provides that funds shall be available to pay Canada's contribution to the work of the united nations relief and rehabilitation administration, a work which has captured the imagination of civilized people everywhere
throughout the world. UNRRA, as it is called, is a partnership of the united nations- the first to be formed. Its aim is to form a community chest to help the nations that are liberated from the enemy to help themselves. UNRRA naturally follows mutual aid, and that is why the two are dealt with in one bill. Victory cannot be won only with the defeat of the enemy. The provision of relief to the people of Europe and Asia who are liberated by the arms of our soldiers and our allies is part of the victory for which we are fighting. Their rehabilitation is part of the victory for which we are fighting. These two great objects form one part of the total defeat of our enemies in this war and in the peace- in war our enemies are Germany and Japan; in the peace, the enemies are fear and poverty and want.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the sum of S800 million suggested for the provision of war-time mutual aid may seem to some too large, while others believe that it is not enough. I hold the view that this amount falls far short of what it is Canada's interest at this time to give her allies. In fighting this war we pay for the clothing, the food and the weapons of our soldiers. This is a fact that is obvious to everyone, but what has not yet become clear to many is that we also have to supply these needs to those people who are fighting the common enemy. A Canadian fighting in France to-day, having beside him a British soldier or a Frenchman, would be only too happy to see that man with the finest equipment, to help him in the battle of liberation. That is the way we have to look at the problem of mutual aid.
I appreciate the words of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George when he spoke of the humanitarian approach rather than the approach of those who give us cold figures to show what we could do with the money. There is one little thing they forget, that there is a war on and that the war has to be fought to the end, to victory; otherwise we shall have very little. War business as usual, I am very happy to see, is not making the grade in this war, and because we refused to allow the old methods of the last war to act as a brake on our war effort we naturally decided on mutual aid. Our population is
11,000,000 in three million square miles and we are short of military man-power for its defence, but we have a very large productive capacity to aid others who are fighting the same enemy. What was physically possible had to be made financially possible and this mutual aid was our answer, a war-time necessity.

Mutual Aid

According to the statement made by the. Minister of Finance (Mr. Xlsley), expenditures for war supplies transferred to Britain in the course of last year amounted to $724,000,000 out of a total of $913,000,000. According to the same statement, a further quantity of munitions amounting to $90,000,000 was purchased by Britain through drawing on the funds she had previously paid into the munitions production revolving fund, and another $165,000,000 of equipment was purchased by the British government through selling their interests in Canad.an plants. Thus, we actually sent to various united nations munitions and other materials amounting to a sum away beyond the one billion dollars. The present figure is $800,000,000, allowing $77,000,000 for UNRRA-quite a reduction.
I ask the house, why the reduction at this time? When men of the united nations are involved in the hardest of the battles, why should we at this time decide that this reduction is justifiable? Materials will be expended at a great rate and we should have no illusions. We have still to learn the amount of material that will be needed. We have learned the lesson of Cassino. At Cassino we learned that planes are good but that we need more and more guns and shells; hence we had suddenly to step up production of guns and shells. We learned at Sicily that we need a lot of automotive equipment. We were short of trucks and many other vehicles and we decided to step up production.
It is better to have more than less. We cannot afford to start learning lessons at this time. The nazi war machine has not yet unleashed its full counter attacks. We do not know what it will be, but we expect that it will come; and the Germans, who still have the European production machine at their disposal, must be met with more powerful material. For that reason the reduction is not justifiable.
The report of the minister notes that war supplies transferred to Britain amounted to $724,000,000; to Russia, $23,000,000; to Australia, $21,000,000, and to China, $4,000,000. In view of the enormous scope of the Soviet and Chinese war efforts, what was allocated to the forces of those nations appears remarkably small. It is natural, because of our closer relations with the British and of earlier placements of war orders in this country, that they should receive the largest share of mutual aid. It scarcely seems logical, however, that Canada should continue in the position of debtor to Britain. In the matter of this indebtedness, I want to quote from a statement of the Minister of Finance to this house on March 18, 1942:
[Hr. Rosed
I have not the accurate figures, but there are Canadian dollar securities still owned in the United Kingdom having an approximate value of $700,000,000. Also there are certain sterling securities on or in Canadian property and enterprises which may have a value of something like $300,000,000.
Prior to the billion-dollar gift to Britain which preceded last year's Mutual Aid bill, this country financed British purchases of munitions by repatriating $700,000,000 of Canadian securities. Without stinting anything to the British, I still cannot see why we stopped short there, why we stopped repatriating Canadian securities.
In connection wdth our expenditures on mutual aid, I wish to say a few words about certain isolationist elements in the province of Quebec who are loud in their condemnation of any contribution to help the allies in fighting the common enemy. They cynically call themselves nationalists, although they should be the first ones to know that if the. nazis had won the battle of Europe, even if they had not crossed over here, the situation for all peoples would have been a terrific one, and French Canadians would have been among those to lose all the rights they have at the present time. What is more, I have heard them here on a number of occasions complaining of a few workers having been sent away from a war factory somewhere in a town in Quebec. I do not understand such logic. If you do not want any war orders; if you do not want to give help to anyone, why do you complain when a few people have to be laid off because of curtailment in production or because of certain changes in types of shells in Bouchard or somewhere else? What gives work to some people in Montreal and elsewhere in the province of Quebec? What gives work to aircraft workers at Noorduyn, Vickers and Fairchild?
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
