subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, mutual aid has given work to many people in the province of Quebec. The aluminum sent to our allies came from the Arvida area, the guns from Dominion Engineering and Sorel Industries, the shells from the Cherrier and Buochard filling plants, wireless apparatus from Marconi, RCA-Victor and Northern Electric, the tanks from the Angus shops and Montreal Locomotive, and clothing from many of the clothing plants throughout the province. Yes, mutual aid has given work to the people, and they have no

Mutual Aid
kick coming in that regard. Are they opposed to the idea of this aid, as some of the isolationists try to make out? I should like to give this house an example to show that the people of Quebec are just as conscious of the need of aiding the allies on behalf of Canada as is anyone else. Some time ago there was a campaign in aid of Russia, during which a collection was taken up at the Angus shops in Montreal, where the greater percentage of the workers are French-Canadians. In the course of a few days they gave, out of their own pockets, some S3,400. They have no complaints about mutual aid.
Unfortunately, however, there is a small but loud group whose hatred, I would say, of the British people and whose love for isolationism blind them to the realities of life. The great patriots of Quebec were not anti-British. I recall the letter sent by the committee of patriots, signed by Louis Joseph Papineau, in which he told the British people that he had no quarrel with them. He differentiated between certain ruling groups and the British people themselves. Unfortunately some people in my province fail to make that distinction at the present time. They claim to be antiimperialists, but they never had any objection to Mussolini's conquests. Less than two years ago Henri Bourassa spoke of Mussolini's Italy as the great Christian nation. Our troops now in that countiy have since found out what poverty and corruption exist there. So that I submit, Mr. Speaker, that these people, these so-called nationalists, are doing the people of Quebec a great injustice when in their name they try to oppose the idea of mutual aid.
There is another aspect of mutual aid this year; that is, the aspect of UNRRA, to which our contribution will be 877,000,000, much of which will be spent in this country in addition to other cash purchases by our allies made with the approval of UNRRA. These purchases should not be limited to wheat but should include clothing and other articles in order that employment may be given to people in the province of Quebec.
We know that mutual aid is necessary for victory, but mutual aid also can become a pattern for the post-war period, a new relationship between nations. In this connection I should like to quote from a radio speech by the United States under-secretary of state, Edward Stettinius, who said:
Lend-lease operations, as we know them, now, will some day draw to a close, but we know already that the principle of mutual aid in mutual self-interest that is embodied in the lend-lease act must live on. To-day there is more unity of purpose and of action among freedom-loving peoples than ever before. In that unity we can find the strength to build the peaceful world in which freedom and opportunity 'will be secure for all.
100-2381	:ur im
It should be remembered that UNRRA does not cover reconstruction of the devastated regions of the world. When this stage is reached our country will be well prepared. We are well equipped to play a leading role, since traditionally we are a great producer of the raw materials necessary for the reconstruction of devastated industrial areas and the tremendous industrial development that is impending in countries such as China. This war has enormously increased our capacity as a builder of capital goods and machine tools. These goods and these tools will be required in vast quantities by China, the Soviet Union and great sections of western Europe. The United States and Great Britain have already obtained some of that business.
In this connection I wish to deal with the idea advanced by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth). Shades of R. B. Bennett! We will provide our people with employment through tariffs! We will start hollering about dumping! We did it before, in 1930. We will say that we are protecting our workers through tariffs! No; if we cannot find a better relationship, for which the pattern has been provided by mutual aid, we are heading for bankruptcy. However, I am very glad that the vast majority of the Canadian people do not think the way the hon. member has expressed himself. Countries that buy machines from us and become industrialized will become good customers of Canada. In the past our best customers have always been the more developed countries, not the backward ones. By helping to develop these countries we will help the people who will buy from us. The hon. member was afraid that the $23,000,000 spent on mutual aid to Russia might have covered some machinery which might be used to dump goods in Canada. In a country that has fought on a two thousand mile front, that has used vast numbers of tanks, planes and other equipment, our $23,000,000 worth of equipment which could not have included very much machinery, is not going to change the situation to any large extent. If we are fearful of that little, how can we have the correct approach to a better, more united world which will give employment to the people of Canada? In connection with this new pattern I mentioned and the new approach we must have, I should like to quote from the New York Times of May 5, which contained this report:
A soviet trade commission is at present conducting negotiations with British business interests for large post-war deliveries similar to those for which orders totalling two and a half billion, dollars already have been placed
Mutual Aid

in the United States.. It is understood, furthermore, that these United States orders are only the beginning of what Russia hopes to do.
Russia's population is so great, the devastation of war has been so vast and the country's supplies are so exhausted that two and a half billion dollars will not even begin to meet her needs. . . .
As to how Russia intends to pay for these purchases, it is understood that the soviet government intends to collaborate fully in the creation of post-war machinery designed to facilitate international trade and monetary payments.
We must take part in this trade and not stand aside. It is not going to wait for us; it will take place just the same. The mutual aid of to-day, but mutual aid to a greater extent, is the path along which we must travel in order to cement relations that will give us a share of such necessary foreign trade. There can be little doubt that when we come to trading, after victory, which I hope is close, we shall be trading with countries in such a state of disorganization that it w'ill be found practicable to deal with governments in stricken countries, rather than with firms. Mutual aid, again, shows the way.
I have dealt with this process of transition, because I sincerely believe that in mutual aid and UNRRA we have that thread which leads on to the next stage-peace-time trade. There are two sides to mutual aid. The allimportant one is that of providing our share in the war against the axis. And, next, it provides one of the most important means of achieving for Canada, and to a considerable degree for other countries, that volume of international trading required for a higher standard of living in the post-war world, a world where Canadians foresee a fuller life than has ever before been theirs. The people of Quebec, with the trades that they have learned and the technique and skills that they have acquired, want to participate to-day through mutual aid, and to-morrow in time of peace in the building of such a world.
I have made these remarks, sincerely believing that we have to find a new' and broader approach. The thinking of the past is obsolete. People who refuse to change will be left far behind by the locomotive of history.
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): Mr. Speaker, I venture to suggest that, in spite of some of the speeches we have heard this afternoon on second reading, this bill will not consecrate any new principle. It is my suggestion that the bill is merely one more step in carrying out the policy which has been that of this country since the early days of September, 1939. If I may be permitted to say so, shortly after I became a member of the government I sat in the Speaker's gallery,

and listened to the exposition of the policy of the government with respect to the war effort of this country.
If I may refer to Hansard of those days, I would recall to members what was then enunciated as the policy the government intended to follow. I would first of all direct the attention of hon. members to page 33 of Hansard for January 26, 1942, where the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said:
At the very outset of the war, the Canadian government considered with the British government the broad lines of development and of our war effort. We tried to envisage all the possibilities of a conflict, which we realized might last for years, and which might spread throughout the world.
The Prime Minister then went on to say:
As I have said already, the policy of the government is, and from the outset has been, the achievement of a total national effort for total wrar. I propose, now, to explain exactly what I understand by the total effort of a nation. It involves two fundamentals.
The first of these is the devotion to the prosecution of the war of all the available energies and resources of the nation in excess of those required to maintain the health and efficiency of the people.
And a little further down:
The foundation of the total effort of any country is a correct decision as to the minimum requirements of the civilian population. Once that is determined, production and consumption except for war, must be steadily and progressively cut down to the minimum. Waste must be eliminated; the manufacture of all luxuries and many comforts must cease. The surplus of man-power and resources thus secured must be used to make war.
. . . Indeed, the most difficult task in total war is the decision of the correct balance between different aspects of the war effort.
Then, the Prime Minister went on to enumerate the activities of the armed forces of the country. If I may quote again, from page 34:
The Canadian navy -has a share in this primary responsibility for our territorial defence. . . . We know, too, that the possibility of finally crushing Hitler depends upon keeping open the sea lanes from North America to Britain and Europe. From the outset, the government -has -placed no limit on -the expansion o-f Canada's navy.
Then, dealing with the army:
The army shares with the navy the responsibility for our territorial defence. It shares also with the navy in the defence of Newfoundland and other islands in the Atlantic. Its main task, however, has been its contribution to the defence of Britain. Every Canadian will remember with pride what Mr. Churchill has said on more than one occasion, of the sense of security which the presence of our -troops has given to the government and people of Britain.

Mutual Aid
And a little further down:
While prepared to send overseas as large an army as Canada can support, without failing in other directions, the government is even more anxious to see that every man, every unit, and the army as a whole, will have the greatest possible striking power.
Then with regard to the air force:
The Royal Canadian Air Force, like the navy and the army, has its part in our territorial defence and the defence of Newfoundland. Its responsibilities on the Pacific coast have been increased by the outbreak of war with Japan. But its main task is the administration of the British commonwealth air training plan. The battle of Britain in 1940 completely justified the emphasis which, from the opening days of the w'ar, Britain and Canada alike placed upon the achievement of air superiority. . . .
The safety of Britain, and Britain's capacity to strike back at the enemy, depends alike upon the air strength concentrated in Britain.
Then, going on with the other aspect of the total war effort:
A vital aspect of Canada's war effort is our contribution to the food supply of Great Britain. This contribution has grown steadily in importance. Britain cannot feed herself, and her own great and growing armed forces. Still less can she feed the ever-increasing numbers of men we are sending from Canada.
Then, with respect to the implements of warfare:
It is well to remember that every battle which has been lost in this war has been lost because of the lack of machines; of planes, or tanks, or guns, or ships. The cry we continue to hear from every front is not so much for numbers of men as it is for tanks, for planes and for ships.
In making the machines of war, Canada's productive task has only begun when our own armed forces have been supplied. Except for planes, Canada has been a main source of British supplies, outside Britain herself.
Then, a little further on we find this, at page 35:
While it cannot be said too often that total war demands total effort, it cannot Ire too strongly emphasized that total effort means using men and resources, where each will count for most, not where their employment will fit in with individual wishes or the wishes of those who have failed to see the needs of our effort as a whole.
That was the programme put before the house, before parliament and the country, and on February 19 I had the privilege of making my first bow to you, Mr. Speaker, of taking my seat in the house, and within an hour of voting with those who supported the administration-among them, and then a member of the administration, the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin)-on the programme which had then been enunciated to the house.
It is my submission that the bill now before the house is merely one further step in implementing that programme of total warfare. It is unnecessary to repeat what has been so well said by other hon. members who have spoken in the debate-notably the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman).
This bill does not provide for a gift to anyone; it provides for the financing of part of the productive capacity of this country in order that that capacity may be devoted to the making of instruments and implements which will serve our cause in overcoming our enemy. Because it is our enemy. In 1939 Canada went to war; the whole of Canada went to war. The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres will allow me to refer to as perhaps a3 eloquent words as were uttered at that time about Canada's going to war. I should like to quote from page 895 of Hansard of June 18, 1940, on the occasion of the second reading of the National Resources Mobilization Act, where the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres is reported as follows:
It has been stated just now that if we are now called upon to vote on a measure of this kind it is because we have made the mistake, in the past year, of taking part in the European conflict. I cannot understand anyone expressing such an opinion and I cannot understand how, when attempting 'to voice the opinion of the province of Quebec, one can so give the lie to the vote given during the recent provincial elections and during the last federal election. . . .
The hon. member went on to say:
The people of my province possessed enough vision, enough intelligence to realize that by restricting their participation to the defence of the Canadian soil only, their participation should prove of no avail, that it would prove fruitless whenever Britain and France were crushed. At such a time, rhetorical, high-sounding speeches and empty words concerning the defence of Canada shall partake only of the theatrical and shall be devoid of any quality of true patriotism to ibe found among men whose main preoccupation is to forestall possible threatening dangers and to prepare, as intelligent men, for the defence of the country.
The hon. member then discussed whether or not the mobilization act provided only for the marshalling of the man-power of the country or of all its resources, and in dealing with objections raised in these words:
. . . with this extravagant war effort on the part of our country, we are going to bankrupt Canada, and to jeopardize our financial stability, we shall run into considerable difficulties and perhaps put ourselves in the position of being unable to provide for the reestablishment of our soldiers after the war.
The hon. member commented as follows:
I have much respect for the hon. member, but I cannot have much respect for such an argument. . . . What will ,be the value of our petty chattels and even of our great assets,
Mutual Aid

what will become of our accumulated wealth if Germany succeeds in crushing under her bloodstained boot the combined strength of France and England? What will become of our savings, and of the money deposited in the banks or invested in industrial plants if the military power of France and England is annihilated? Our so-called wealth will be worth as much as that of Poland, of Czechoslovakia, our so-called assets will have just the value that those of Holland, Norway and Belgium have to-day.
That is how the problem should be faced. During the last election I stated many times, in the province of Quebec something which X am not afraid to maintain before the people, before every one of my fellow-citizens: Money is of no importance when the freedom of a nation is at stake.
This afternoon the hon. member said that he found it strange that a little country like ours should be called upon to make gifts to a country much older and*much richer. He described the power and influence of the British empire and asked if that great empire were not capable of taking care of its obligations. I submit that the obligation of that country to mankind and to the cause of humanity has been well taken care of since the days of Dunkirk.
But let us come down to the plane of material things. The hon. member says that possibly that country has expended its dollar credits in the purchase of the things required to make war in the cause of all freedom-loving people, but that later on it might be able to pay. Have we not all learned that the things called dollars or sterling or pounds are merely symbols, that any true payment can be made only in material things which would have to be exported from the British isles to this country if there were a debt to be repaid to us?
Do we as representatives of the Canadian people want to see the stagnation of our own productive capacity in order that we may use things made and provided by countries beyond our borders? During the years of war, in addition to the self-respect of freedom-loving men throughout the world we have acquired a much better knowledge of our own productive capacity and of the things that we can make available for our own people and even for export to others. Would it not be a major disaster if anything should occur after the cessation of hostilities to make it impossible to use the productive capacity, the experience and the skill we have developed during this war to provide those things which can be used to the advantage of our population.
I should like to refer again to the words of the hon. member, as reported on page 897 of Hansard of 1940. Speaking of the purchase and sale of implements of warfare, he said:
I have no use for that kind of patriotism which would limit itself to selling produce, 
materials and arms, in short, to making money without accepting the responsibility of a free and independent people.
Doubtless we can help the cause of liberty and democracy by supplying arms to England and her allies; doubtless we can help them by sending them as much as possible in the way of munitions and foodstuffs; but I ask those who bring forward this argument: Do you not in your heart feel a bit ashamed of thinking only in terms of money while abandoning to your neighbours the protection of your life, of your possessions and of your rights!
Knowing the hon. member as it has been my privilege to know him, knowing what a doughty fighter he has been throughout the whole of his brilliant career, I ask myself whether he would pull his punches in the midst of a critical fight. I do not think so, and I do not think in all sincerity he would ask this country to pull its punches at this time.
The hon. member dealt with some of the arguments which he said had been put forward to support other measures of this kind and said that he could not put much stock in the argument that by making this amount available to the treasury in order to pay for munitions and supplies purchased in this country we were providing markets for our farmers and work for that part of our population which labours in our factories, in our shipyards and in our other war plants. He suggested that this might be done as well by devoting their energy to the production of the things we could use at home. That may be quite true. But would that be making total war? And are we or are we not at this stage going back on the policy which was endorsed by the whole Canadian people, which was for a total war effort?
The hon. member says, where else are measures of this kind being adopted? They are being adopted, of course, in the United States. They had been adopted there even before the American people became engaged in shooting warfare. But where else could they be adopted? Where else were there opportunities for producing more than the armed forces of the country engaged required? To a certain extent that was true of Britain and it is true also of New Zealand and Australia. But is it not, as was suggested by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman), the privilege of this young nation that it was so placed by Providence that a very effective part of its effort in the war was performed in its forests, on its farms, in its mines and factories and plants? If it be true that this country had pledged to itself as well as to the other united nations a total war effort for the safety and security of its own population, was it not required that everything which was not neces-

Mutual Aid
sary for the maintenance of the health and productive capacity of our population be devoted to the common cause?
The hon. member says that we were not attacked, as the United States were, that there was no Pearl Harbor which brought us into the conflict. May I suggest that the actual entry of our neighbours to the south into the war was just as inevitable from, its very outbreak as it appeared to the majority of the people to be after the onslaught of the Japanese on Pearl Harbor in December, 1941. It requires no effort of imagination now to understand what the President of the United States had in mind in 1936 when he proclaimed that the United States was a peace-loving nation, that they were at peace with th,eir nieghbours but that they were capable of defending and willing to defend themselves and would defend themselves and their whole neighbourhood; when he repeated the same warning in 1938 and even more pointedly said that if any other foreign country ever attempted to dominate any part of Canadian soil the American people would not stand idly by. Was that not a warning to the whole world that the government of the United States recognized the imminence of possible warfare and was endeavouring to deter the aggressors from their bellicose designs by warning them that no part of this continent could become a prey to their cupidity without their first overthrowing the combined might of the United States and of Canada and of those who might be allied to Canada?
The hon. member says that it was argued by my predecessor in this house that when Great Britain was at war Canada could not remain neutral. It is quite apparent to every Canadian that when the United Kingdom is in the kind of war that this is, self-respecting Canadians cannot remain neutral. But technically is there any difference in the legal position of this dominion and that of the Irish Free State, where those who feel so inclined can remain neutral when the United Kingdom and the rest of the British commonwealth are at war? But I put it to this house, and fearlessly put it to this country, how many in this country prefer the attitude adopted in the Irish Free State to the attitude that has been adopted by the Canadian people?

subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Not very many.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres goes on and says that he does not object to the producing of food and the implements of wrarfare, but that he would insist upon accounts being kept. Within the last few days the allied forces have been able to liberate the city of Rome, something which has a very special meaning to a great many of
the citizens of this country, whether they be of my faith or of other Christian faith; the allied forces have now set foot on the western shores of the continent of Europe and we can foresee the liberation from the nazi yoke of the peoples of that continent.
In the same address the hon. member, whose eloquence I would not attempt to approach, spoke of France, in these words:
Allow me to tell him, Mr. Speaker, that France, poor France, is agonizing at the present time.
May I suggest that France is, four years afterwards, "hoping," at the present time.
He went on:
She has always stood, down the course of history, as a shining beacon illuminating the progress of ideas and principles throughout the world, and has spared neither sacrifice nor the life of her sons in the defence of freedom, in protecting the weak and the humble. She has ever been in the forefront of spiritual progress, of intellectual development and of liberty. Poor France, she has suffered down through the ages because of her .principles and of her noble feelings of humanity. She lias just put up such a valiant struggle as to prove even the humblest soldier of her powerful army a hero. One after the other, by the hundreds and by the thousands, they have fallen on the battlefields and have been crushed by the barbarian Hitler's powerful war machine. They have fallen in defence of humanity, in defence of human liberties, yours and mine, my friends.
France is now at the dawn of the day when she will rise again and continue throughout the ages the noble traditions so eloquently spoken of by the hon. member. That I suggest is not the day when accounts should be kept. Has France kept account of the sufferings she has undergone since her Gethsemane of four years ago? All those sufferings and sacrifices of freedom-loving peoples constitute a part of the assets placed in the common pool for the redemption of free mankind, and I suggest that the first lines on page 9 of the report of the Canadian mutual aid board express the true situation in this regard:
The sacrifices of allied soldiers, sailors and airmen transcend any form of material aid. The weighing of lives against munitions cannot *be made in a report. It must be made in the [DOT]heart and conscience of every Canadian.
There is not that unanimous degree of unity throughout this country that all of us here in this house would wish for, but there is a considerable degree of unanimous feeling in that regard, and in my own city of Quebec it was expressed by two eloquent voices immediately after the opening of the invasion on the west coast of France. The newly-appointed Anglican Archbishop of Quebec, His Grace Archbishop Phillip Carrington, said, on June 7:
We have a right to pray to God for a blessing upon the terrible work which we have under-
Mutual Aid

taken. Let us pray that it may be done wisely and firmly. Let us pray that it may be done quickly. Let us pray that we may remain true to those ideals for which we have banded ourselves together; let us pray that the evil may be overcome, the oppressed set free, justice and freedom established, peace and prosperity restored.
And the night before, His Eminence Cardinal Villeneuve had broadcast throughout the country and caused to be published this message:
At this moment, as allied forces, after having liberated the Eternal City, are establishing a foothold on French soil preparatory to unburdening the continent of the four-year nazi yoke, I invite all Catholics in Canada to offer their sacrifices and prayers in order that God may inspire our leaders and help our soldiers in this supreme phase of the war. . . .
Let us take confidence in the message of Saint Augustine; may our prayers be heard by He who governs all, for, in time of battle, the gates of heaven are open, and God looks upon the battle-fields, reserving victory for he whose cause is just.
We believed in 1939 that the cause of the allied nations was just. We believed it to the extent of pledging our people to a total war effort until a total victory; and the second reading of this bill is merely designed to implement our continued determination that this country shall make total war until total victory has been achieved.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1942, this government made to England an outright gift of one billion dollars. In 1943, they gave a further gift of one billion dollars to the United Nations and again this year they are about to give 8800,000,000. If we add to that the loan of 8700,000,000 made to England without interest we have a grand total of
83,500,000,000, or 867,000,000 more than the total debt of this country from confederation to August 31, 1939, when war was declared. What a far cry that is from the 1940 pledges according to which we are to confine ourselves to a moderate war effort. We have been giving billions of dollars since 1942. Well, Mr. Speaker, I say that the government have no right to give away the people's money, they have no mandate to do so, because it was through the promise of a moderate war effort Jiat they were returned in 1940. Now, strangely enough, on May 11 last, our prime minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said in a speech delivered before the Westminster Parliament;
Our objective has been a total effort for total war, and we believe that objective is being attained.
_ Mr. Speaker, I wonder what thoughts such gifts suggest to workers who have large families^ to support, who lack some of the necessaries of life, Who are not properly housed [Mr. St. Laureot.l
and who reflect that a sum of 8800,000,090 represents 870 for each member of their families. And our farmers are no more in a position to make such gifts; they were requesting the government's help during the depression years of 1930-1939, but they always had the same answer: "We have no money." They will be surprised to hear that since 1942 the government have given outright 82,800,000,000, which represents 8240 per capita and 81,920 for a family of eight persons. We believe that such a policy is prejudicial to the interests of Canada and we unequivocally oppose it. No other nation within the British empire votes such appropriations. Our contribution in maintaining our armed forces is quite considerable and Canada has such a large debt that it cannot afford to make such gifts to countries very much wealthier than ours.
Mr. Speaker, the honourable member for Montreal-Car,tier (Mr. Rose) has seen fit to lecture the French-Canadian members from the province of Quebec who are opposed to gifts of 81,000,000,000 and 8800,000,000 to other nations. I for one believe that the province of Quebec has done its duty in the past to preserve Canada for Canadians on each occasion when the country was threatened. The French Canadians are just as patriotic as the other citizens of this country and they will remain so in opposing any policy that is prejudicial to Canada's interests.
Mr. J. EMMANUEL d'ANJOU (Rimouski) (Translation); Mr. Speaker, I shall contribute but a few words to the current debate on the bill under discussion. I have already condemned the tribute we are requested to vote, in my speech on the address, on February 3rd last. I shall quote some of my remarks as recorded on Hansard of that date:
The speech from the throne again hints at the government's intention to authorize, in the course of the present session, the payment of another tribute of a billion dollars to Great Britain. I state right now, Mr. Speaker, that I shall oppose this measure with all my strength, as I have done on two previous occasions.
Instead of paying an annual tribute to England, the government would be far better inspired in endeavouring to relieve the distress which is to be met all over the country.
Once more I state my opposition to the present bill still more forcibly, if that- is possible. I oppose the measure submitted to the house at this moment as I have the last two similar bills. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I deem it would be wiser on the part of the government to endeavour to assuage the sufferings of our own population than to give, at each session, gifts to England, a country which, at the time we paid our first tribute, was making interest bearing loans to China.

Mutual Aid
In my constituency, there are sections where destitution is prevalent. The government would evidence a greater concern for the interests of the country in attempting to alleviate the poverty of these people. When we paid our first tribute to England, I denounced it with the utmost energy; I held the same attitude in connection with the second tribute and I am still of the same mind on this third occasion. Therefore, if we are called upon to vote on this measure, I shall vote against it, as I have done in the past.
I was listening, a while ago, to the speech delivered by the hon. member for Montreal-Cartier (Mr. Rose). He criticized the members from Quebec who oppose war measures and especially the bill now submitted to the approval of the house. The representatives from Quebec who, in this house, show enough courage to fulfil their duty, to discharge their responsibility toward the electors of their constituencies, have no lesson to learn from the hon. member for Montreal-Cartier.
At a time when the country admits Jewish refugees, when families land here 70 or 80 at a time, the hon. member for Montreal-Cartier should not assail the hon. members from Quebec. The hon. member for Montreal-Cartier said: "We must win the war, and if we lose it, it will be the fault of the dissident members of the province of Quebec; if we lose the war, the rights of French Canadians might be imperilled".
I do not think Jewish rights are threatened because under the constitution of Canada, they are guaranteed none. To my mind, it ill behooves the member for Montreal-Cartier in parliament to disparage French Canadians of the province of Quebec when in his own constituency the French-Canadian population is quite numerous, and when a few of our fellow-citizens, probably misguided, voted for him in the last election.
I will add nothing further, Mr. Speaker. As I said before, I am opposing the bill now before the house; I want to be logical, and I believe my constituents will admit that, since 1940, I have maintained a logical stand and have fulfilled the pledges given to the electors of my constituency. The hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) said a while ago that we had to fight an all-out war. I remember that in 1940, during the last election, the predecessor of the present Minister of Justice, the lamented Mr. Lapointe, told the province of Quebec: "Participation in the war will be free, voluntary, and moderate". In 1940, total war was not advocated in the province of Quebec. It was stated that participation would be free, voluntary and moderate. To-day, we are told that the
country has approved total participation in the war. The people were trustful and they gave their allegiance to the Liberal party believing that party would keep its pledges and promises honourably; but they were odiously deceived. Mr. Speaker, I will add nothing more; once again, I condemn this measure and I will vote against it.

Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata):	I listened with great attention to
the eloquent speech made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent). We must not be under the impression that those who discuss this measure are not in favour of the prosecution of the war and of helping the allied nations. Not at all. The only thing, and it is a legitimate feeling, is that the Canadian taxpayer expects tl\at as soon as the armistice is signed the burden of taxation will be less, that it will not be so heavy; and that is the very reason why Canadians have agreed to bear the heavy burden of taxation which is now imposed upon all of us. It is in the expectation that after the war that taxation will become less. One way to achieve such a result is precisely by discussing this matter with other nations on business terms.
There is no one in this house who refuses to give credit to the allied nations. The only thing that is asked for is an acknowledgment. On June 2, 1941, the hon. member for Temis-couata spoke as follows:
My last remark is that we should not consider taxation as though the war were .being lost. We are all determined to win t'he war, but taxation must be related to our needs. At the [DOT]present time taxation is just the same as though the deluge were coming to-morrow

"after us, the deluge." Taxation should ibe clear, progressive and in accordance with the means of the people.
Now let us see what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) said about the record regarding the past:
. . . when we are proposing to open a new chapter in our financial relations-
With Great Britain and the United States.
*-the record regarding the past should be made quite clear.
That statement of the minister was made on March 18, 1942, when the house was considering for the first time the billion dollar gift, United Kingdom financing. The Minister of Finance said:
To the United Kingdom alone our shipments increased from $331 million in 1939 to $532 million in 1940 and $702 million in 1941. To the rest of the British empire, including Egypt, our shipments rose from $104 million in 1939 to $157 million in 1940 and $300 million in 1941. . . . But notwithstanding some increase in our imports,-

Mutual Aid

The minister did not mention what our imports were then. I had to make a calculation and I sent him my mathematical work on the matter.
[DOT]-the empire as a whole had an aggregate merchandised deficit with Canada of $445 million in 1940 and $723 million in 1941.
AVhat was the financial assistance of Canada to the British' empire? The Minister of Finance went on:
Nor does this empire deficit of nearly $1,200 million on trade account in the past two years tell the whole story. In addition, large sums have been required for expenditures not reflected in the trade statistics.
And I have numbered each one.
(1) The most important of these have been the British capital investments in war plants in Canada, amounting at the end of 1941 to $238 million, and (2) British expenditures in connection with air training activities in Canada. (3) In addition, of course, there have been other expenses, such as for freight and (4) storage connected with the movement of goods within Canada.
Without going into exhaustive details, I may inform the house that after making allowance for all the sterling area's receipts of Canadian dollars of a current or ordinary nature-such as (a) the proceeds of exports, (b) interest and (c) dividend receipts, (d) shipping receipts and (e) Canadian governmental expenditures in sterling incurred in connection with the maintenance of our troops in the United Kingdom-* the sterling area's net deficit of Canadian dollars from the outbreak of the war until the end of February. 1942, amounted to approximately $1,770 million.
What was the financing by Canada of the sterling areas net deficit of $1,770 million? Let me quote the Minister of Finance again, but before coming to that I may say that the minister's summary of Canadian expenditures was incomplete because it did not include payments for prisoners of war, et cetera. I quote the minister:
This deficit has been financed in three ways. In increasing order of importance they are: (1) gold payments from the United Kingdom to Canada: (2) redemption or purchase, mainly in advance of maturity, of Canadian security obligations held in the United Kingdom; and (3) the accumulation of sterling finances held by the foreign exchange control board on deposit in London.
Then the minister spoke of the whole of the sterling area deficit having been financed by Ottawa out of its own resources, which is almost incredible. He said:
Gold payments by the United Kingdom have amounted to $250,000,000 over this whole period. As the house is aware, the last payment was received in December, 1940, and since that time the whole of the sterling area deficit has .been financed by Ottawa out of its own resources.
Think of that.
Over the period as a whole gold payments have covered less than fifteen per cent of the sterling area deficit in Canada.

Not only have gold payments by the United Kingdom been kept to relatively modest proportions, but every ounce of gold we obtained from the United Kingdom was promptly converted into United States funds and used to pay for LTnited States goods needed to complete w*ar orders for the United Kingdom.
That is what the minister said; and he went on:
Exact statistics are not available, but there can be no doubt whatever that the amounts we have paid out in United States exchange in connection with British war orders in Canada are very greatly in excess of the amount of hard currency settlement received from the United Kingdom.
It was neither the leader of any opposition group nor any private member who might be accused by the imperialist press of being an isolationist; it was the Minister of Finance who declared that gold payments by the United Kingdom had covered less than fifteen per cent of the sterling area deficit in Canada, and commented that they had been kept to relatively modest proportions. And think of this, sir. Since December, 1940, according to the word of the Minister of Finance, we have taken the whole burden on our shoulders. He said:
Until December, 1940, the United Kingdom shared with us the burden of providing the necessary hard currency. Since then we have taken the whole burden on our own shoulders. The burden has not been a light one.
Those were the words of the Minister of Finance. That date, December, 1940, is of the utmost importance. First, it was the month in which Canada received the last gold payment from the United Kingdom; second, it was when the United Kingdom ceased "to share with us the burden of providing the necessary hard currency," and, third, that was when we "took the whole burden on our shoulders." Then the minister added that the burden had not been a light one. Naturally the burden of financing the whole sterling area could not have been a light one. Here is another important quotation from the speech made by the Minister of Finance on that occasion:
. . . our United States dollar problem and our need of foreign exchange control are in part a direct consequence of our assistance to Great Britain.
Then a most unusual thing occurred; the minister went so far as to express deep concern about the result of the financial policies he had been sponsoring. He said:
I warned the house in introducing the budget last April-
That was 1940.
-that the need for United States exchange conservation had not passed .	.	. and lest
anyone should think that the Hyde Park agree-

Mutual Aid
ment has solved our United States dollar exchange problem, I should like to say that our official reserves of gold and United States dollars fell by $142,000,000, United States dollars, in 1941. . . Moreover, although the outlook is far from clear, it must be recognized that, failing remedial action, we appear to be faced with another sizeable loss of reserves this year. . . .
Our United States dollar position is, therefore, still a major cause of concern. . . .
I stress this point because our United States dollar problem and our need of foreign exchange control are in part a direct consequence of our assistance to Great Britain.
At this point the minister made this remark:
When we are proposing to open a new chapter in our financial relations, the record regarding the past should be made quite clear.
It is very important that we understand the statements and the attitude of the Minister of Finance in the matter. The "new chapter in our financial relations" with Great Britain was not "opened", to use the minister's expression, on March 18, 1942, when he made that speech on the United Kingdom financing scheme; it dated back to fifteen months before, to December, 1940, when Great Britain made its last gold payment and when we took "on our own shoulders" the whole burden of financing the sterling area deficit. The minister did not try to escape any responsibility, but he did not make the record regarding the past clear enough. On November 7, 1940, Mr. Purvis was named by the United Kingdom to the new war purchasing mission. The Montreal Gazette of November 8, 1939, carried this item:
Ottawa, November 7-C.P.-Appointment of Arthur B. Purvis, prominent Montreal industrialist, as director general of British war purchases in the United States, was announced here to-night by the British purchasing mission which has been in Ottawa since early September. . . .
It has already been expressed as a matter of British policy that Canada will be looked upon as a first and primary source of supply to the full extent of the manufacturing and industrial capacity of the dominion.
It is believed purchases in the United States will be limited by the amount of foreign exchange available for that purpose, the extent to which Canada can supply British needs in raw and manufactured materials, and of course the length and proportions of the war.
Replaces Previous Board
The war supply board reached its full status last Wednesday when it took over the functions and personnel of the defence purchasing board set up last July under chairmanship of R. C. Vaughan, vice-president in charge of purchases for the Canadian National Railways.
Created under authority of the War Measures Act, the war supply board will have extraordinary powers to mobilize and regulate industry, production and other resources in Canada for a concentrated war effort.
To what extent these powers will be exercised has not yet been indicated, but a statement covering the board's plan of procedure
100-239J
is expected shortly. Not only Canadian purchases but those for the British government will be handled by the board as agent. Presumably the same would be true of any French orders that might be placed in Canada.
If the task of the supply board assumes proportions indicating the necessity for creation of a ministry of munitions and supply the government is empowered, by an act of the special war session of parliament in September, to set- up the extra portfolio with a full-time minister.
The defence purchasing board was set up under the then Minister of Finance in July, 1939, a short time before Mr. Dunning's resignation and departure for London. It was under his successor in that capacity, the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) and the perpetual Acting Minister of Finance, when it was replaced by the war supply board, with-
.	.	. extraordinary powers to mobilize and
regulate industry, production and other resources in Canada for a concentrated war effort.
When Mr. Purvis was appointed the news appeared in the press more than eight months before the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) introduced the mobilization act in June, 1940.
On November 15, 1940, the Minister of National Defence, who was then Acting Minister of Finance, left for London. On November 15, 1940, the sixth sitting day of the session, the then Minister of National Defence, and also perpetual Acting Minister of Finance, concluded as follows a lengthy speech on the address:
Let me emphasize again that our plans and preparations are and must be made in conjunction with those of our predominating partner, the United Kingdom, and of the other dominions. Since the front line is on the English channel, it is vital that we maintain the closest contact with that crucial sphere of operations. There must he not only unity of purpose but unity of planning and execution. Our strength multiplies by integration. It is teamwork which wins. For this reason I expect before long to visit the United Kingdom, accompanied by some of the headquarters staff, to consult on many matters of common interest. I want to make sure that our own programme will be developed in closest relation to the needs, and I am sure we all desire that plans and preparations will be such that we will be contributing not only all our strength, but our most effective strength, to help defeat and destroy this menace to freedom and to life itself which hangs over the world. It will be a task of years. May we have the courage, the perseverance and the unshakable resolution to see it through.
He left early in the following week.
In December, 1940, he spent a most useful evening with the late Arthur B. Purvis. This appears in Hansard of June 11, 1941, where the Minister of National Defence, and perpetual Acting Minister of Finance, said:
Mr. Purvis was good enough to give me, in the way he can give it quickly, concisely and
Mutual Aid

comprehensively the fullest statement possible with regard to production in the United States and with regard to the needs of Britain with regard to munitions and supplies. I do not know when I spent an evening which was more useful in connection with the work that I was doing, and it gave me an idea of how we could integrate our production with that of the United States, and our needs with the needs of Britain.
He added that he kept that information for his colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe). Neither of them said any more to the house about Mr. Purvis' statement.
The record regarding the past, read in the house by the Minister of Finance on March 18, 1942, makes it clear beyond doubt that the late Mr. Purvis' statement to the Acting-Minister of Finance was the suggestion to finance the whole of the sterling area deficit by Ottawa, out of his own resources. And we may draw the conclusion that it was because it was so promptly accepted by the Acting-Minister of Finance that the Minister of Finance expressed so much concern about it, and went so far as to state that our United States dollar problem and our need of foreign exchange control are, in part, a direct consequence of our financial assistance to Great Britain. He specified that we have taken the whole burden on our shoulders, from December, 1940, the time when the Acting-Minister of Finance spent his most useful evening with the late Mr. Purvis.
Now, sir, this is not the day to speak outside the record. The record is there. I have quoted some of it, and I have more to quote in due course, because I have made a special study of it. There is no one more ready to do anything to assist the united nations in this terrific struggle; but it is a good thing to have an acknowledgment of what is done, because otherwise it will be forgotten. No one is refusing to let the allied nations have all they need from Canada, provided there is acknowledgment of it. I do not find it honest to establish trade balances with gifts made to other countries. Besides that, the government went to all countries both in and outside the British empire, countries whiijh did not need any help of any kind. That help was flatly refused by Bermuda, for instance. Until last year and this year there was no income tax legislation in Bermuda, and the Bermudians were in much better financial condition than we are. They were offered a gift. I wonder how many nations have been offered gifts by this government, nations which do not need it.
There are three kinds of united nations. There are those who need help, and there are those who do not need help or assistance. They are in a class by themselves. The

others need assistance, but some of them have means to pay. If they cannot pay now, they should at least give an acknowledgment. Those who have no means to pay now should also give an acknowledgment for the future. That, I believe, should be the position of all when the rehabilitation of all countries is under consideration. That would apply even to those countries which are occupied by the enemy but which have temporary governments in England at the present time.
We have done a great deal to help Great Britain, and it has been acknowledged in some quarters. I was not a stranger to it, because I missed no opportunity to publicize what has been done by Canada for other countries. Some people, however, have a very strange turn of mind. To-day I happened to see the kind of propaganda issued by the British information services, an agency of the British government with offices at 30 Rockefeller plaza, New York city. This article is headed "The British Commonwealth and Empire," and appears at page 6 in a folder describing the British empire in terms which each member will find insulting. Here is what I find in connection with dominion status.
Thus dominion status is the most advanced stage of ^a process of political evolution or change-like the change from the frog's egg through the tadpole stage to the complete frog. If we had some sixty frogs, tadpoles and frogs' eggs of various ages in a pond, they would change and grow; the eggs .becoming tadpoles; the tadpoles frogs; the frogs growing ibigger and perhaps leaving the pond. At any moment, of course, some would already be changed into frogs; some would still be in the egg, some in the early tadpole stage; and some nearly transformed, but with a rudimentary and fast disappearing tail. Some might be very slow to hatch out of the egg, and others might stay too long in the tadpole stage-but in the end they would all change and grow up. This is a parable of the British commonwealth and empire.
What do you think of it? If we could help the British people, directly, as we have the people of Greece, it would be a very good thing. I have not the least objection to helping those who need help, especially those who are in hunger in occupied Europe. It seems to be the concerted plan of Germany to destroy whole countries. But where a nation is able to pay there should be an acknowledgment. Canada is the only country that is making such gifts, and we have not the means to do so. Taxation is heavy. We are ready to help in the prosecution of the war as far as our means will permit, but now we are doing much more. This legislation is taxing future generations to the limit without any hope of having anything in return. What we want is an

Mutual Aid
acknowledgment of what we are doing, and if it is secured Canada will be in a much better position when the nations meet at the peace conference after the war.

speechtext:
Great Britain does not do that with us and I am inclined to think we should not do it with her. I do not think there is much use in arguing the economics of this matter. It is just a matter of principle; it is the way the people feel. I believe I know how most of the members of this house feel about it and how most of the people of the Dominion of Canada feel about it; I think they believe in the indivisibility of the common cause. They believe that this is not a gift to Great Britain, a gift to (Russia, a gift to Australia or a gift to China. It certainly is not a gift to enrich any of those countries. If it could be regarded in any sense as a gift, it is a gift to enable them to fight a war which is our war just the same as it is their war, and I prefer not to call it a gift at all. I would prefer to consider it a contribution to the common cause. If we believe that in our hearts and minds, there is not very much more to be said on the issue.
I can, I think, dispose fairly quickly of any argument that there would be any economic advantage in taking a lot of sterling from Great Britain or in establishing a huge claim
Mutual Aid

on the books against Great Britain after the war. I believe I could establish pretty well that the only way that a huge intergovernmental debt of that kind could ever be paid would be by vastly decreasing our exports or vastly increasing our imports, or both, and that both these would have to be on such a scale that it is something that we cannot envisage because it would so dislocate and destructively impair our economy that no government would undertake it. If I wanted to put it on an economic basis I could make a good case. But even though I am dealing with finance most of the time, which perhaps is not the very highest plane, I want to put this question on the plane on which the Minister of Justice put it, which is the plane on which a good many members have discussed the question this afternoon and this evening. Certainly I do not believe that this nation could remain a self-respecting nation if it took a course very much different from the course it is taking. It is not an argument to come along and say that some of the other British dominions are not doing this and that we should not follow the United States because the United States is so much wealthier than we are. Let us examine the facts.
I was greatly struck in listening to the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres this afternoon by his tendency to talk about our smallness, our dependence, our insignificance, although he did not use that word, as a nation. He was picturing Canada as so small, dependent on Great Britain, and not able to assume large and important obligations. I do not think of Canada in that- way. I admit that Canada has not a large population. It has a population of eleven or twelve million people. But this country, it must be remembered, is the oldest and largest of the British dominions. It is a country of great potential wealth and great resources. Moreover, it is a country far removed from the scene of conflict. It is a country which has an opportunity of great .production, and certainly it is the duty of this country in time of war to develop that production and contribute it to the common cause.
The other countries have done what they could. The United States of America has, as I said last night, devoted $24 billion to lend-lease up to date, which is a substantial sum. It is not profitable, it is really futile, to compare the per capita expenditure for mutual aid or lend-lease as between countries, because the situation in the different countries varies so greatly that it would be difficult to make an effective comparison. To take just one phase of a country's war expenditures and compare that with what some other country is doing is
[Mr. Hsley.l
not fair. But we do have that very large expenditure for lend-lease in the United States of America.
Then I find from a British white paper which has been issued, called "A Report on Mutual Aid," that the various parts of the British empire have been doing what they could. It would be unreasonable to expect Australia, situated as she is, to make the same per capita contribution as Canada. But let me read paragraph 11 of this British white paper, "A Report on Mutual Aid," presented by the chancellor of the exchequer to parliament by command of His Majesty, November, 1943:
11. His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom are, of course, not responsible for reciprocal aid as between the dominions and the United States. The Australian and New Zealand governments signed reciprocal aid , agreements on the 3rd September, 1942, simultaneously with our own, and have given reciprocal aid at their own expense on a scale which is large in proportion to their resources. The South African government is giving reciprocal aid without any formal agreement; and the same is true of the government of India, who bear the cost of reciprocal aid given to the United States forces in India.
On. the general question of. the pooling of resources I find this in paragraph 4 of this same British white paper:
4. His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom have recognized how greatly mutual aid assists the efficient prosecution of the war and good relations between comrades-in-arms. The principle of the transfer of goods and services without charge or calculation is a necessary part of the efficient planning of the war from the point of view of strategy and the economical use of man-power and shipping. It is, therefore, the policy of His Majesty's government to apply that principle themselves wherever possible, not only to the United States, but also to other allies, and they think it proper to satisfy the public interest in the subject by now reporting to parliament in some detail on the scope of the various arrangements which are in force.
In other words, a great international system of mutual aid has been established in which this country took an early part and an honourable part, to the great credit of this country and to the great benefit of all concerned in the prosecution of this war. No party in this house has ever opposed it. There has been the odd member who has expressed opposition to what we are doing, but I have been struck in this debate by the mildness of the opposition and by the strength of the support which the mutual aid principle has received in the parliament of Canada. I think that is greatly to the credit of the parliament of Canada, just as the support which this principle has received from the Canadian people is greatly to the credit of the Canadian people.

Mutual Aid

I am not surprised to hear Aeolian harps, because the amount is $800,000,000. It is something to consider, and during the election of 1935 I visited Essex South in the campaign against the late Eccles Gott, who was a staunch supporter of the Bennett government and who interrupted me at times. That trip was a very satisfactory one and I also went into Essex county to the support of the present Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty). I am calm. I have something to say and I will say it. On March 17, 1942, speaking of the billion dollar gift, the Minister of Finance spoke as follows:
All I am asking now-and I am putting all my cards on the table-is this: I am saying that for tremendously important reasons I want interim supply, the supplementary appropriations and the one billion dollar bill passed. If the house will do that, they can take the rest of the time, so far as I am concerned, on this matter before the house.
On March 18, 1942, the Minister of Finance introduced a measure to finance the United Kingdom. Canada's net accumulation of sterling balances in London banks from the outbreak of the war to the end of February, 1942, had amounted to $992,000,000. The Minister of Finance stated that the sterling area's, the whole empire's deficit of Canadian dollars for that period amounted to $1,770,000,000, of which $250,000,000 was "financed" by the United Kingdom and nearly $125,000,000 "was privately financed by discharge of private Canadian debts to the United Kingdom including certain sales in the Canadian market of securities vested by the British treasury." The $250 million gold payments by the United Kingdom to Canada and the $125 million sales of Canadian securities vested by
Mutual Aid

the British treasury formed a total of $375 million to be subtracted from what he described as a $1,770 -million deficit. He adds that $1,400 million had been "directly financed by the dominion government-about $400,000,000 through repatriation of securities and nearly $1,000,000,000 through the accumulation of sterling balances in London".
He repeated twice, but with different figures, the same amount of sterling balances: $992 million as a Canadian asset and $1,000 million as a sterling area liability to Canada. Then he explained that Canada had previously purchased British-held Canadian securities amounting to $400 million. Therefore, at the end of February, 1942, Canada had repatriated $400 million securities "to make Canadian dollars available to the British government for its purchases and other expenditures in Canada." That amount of $400 million should also have been subtracted from the balance of sterling area's deficit, leaving a net balance of $1,000 million, or $992 million, which was credited to Canada by the London banks.
His measure was threefold. It provided, first, for the outright gift of $1,000 million for war purchases in Canada; second, for the acceptance by Canada of a $700 million United Kingdom obligation, without interest until the end of the war "in exchange for an equivalent amount of deposits in pounds sterling held in banks in the United Kingdom; third, for the purchase of unmatured dominion or Canadian National Railway securities held by the government of the United Kingdom. The Canadian government was empowered to borrow $1,000 million to purchase said securities, Was it sensible to raise by way of loan $1,000 million to repatriate those securities? Could it not have been done as a matter of course with the idle Canadian credit of a similar amount in the London banks?
With regard to the $700 million United Kingdom obligation, the Minister of Finance said:
It has also been proposed to the British government, and they have agreed, that the tunds arising from any redemption or repayment during the war of Canadian securities owned in Britain will be applied to the reduction ot the loan.
The dominion government made a distinction between the securities, first held by the British government, and second, those owned in Britain. Why was not a similar policy applied to both kinds of securities? Those held by the British government were bearing a low rate of interest of three and1 four per cent. We repatriated a considerable amount of such investments. Those owned in Britain were C.I.L., rayon companies, Enos Fruit Salts, Red Rose Tea, Hudson Bay Company, Inter-
national Nickel, Lever Brothers Soap, et cetera. They were in the hands of a few financial wizards close to the Bank of England and Barclay's bank. Naturally, the latter were much more profitable than the former. They were not repatriated.

If the repatriation policy was the right one for a certain category of securities, was it not for all of them? South Africa easily secured the approval of the British government for the transfer of ownership of the stock of Diamond Gold Mines, which was paid with the credit which that countiy had in the London banks. But the financiers associated with those banks feared that the Canadian government might follow the South African precedent. They had a flea in their ear. They succeeded in convincing the Canadian government to adopt the following scheme to leave their profitable commercial investments untouched. The dominion government accepted from the United Kingdom a $700 million obligation without interest and payable after the war, to be financed with the sterling credit account of Canada in London, which was to be more than covered with a further credit of $1,000 million.

Mutual Aid
The year before Canada had supplied Great Britain with all the foodstuffs and munitions that we could produce.
The Canadian government long ago advised the British prime minister that the United Kingdom could continue to buy in Canada all essential supplies that could be procured and transported without any fear of the shortage of dollars. ... I believe that all Canadians approved the assurance thus given to the government of the United Kingdom. . . . The continuance of these purchases and expenditures, however, involves a continuance of the huge deficit of the sterling area in its balance of payments with Canada which must be financed (very largely at least, perhaps wholly) by Canada itself.
Those were the words of the Minister of Finance. That high finance deal did not benefit the soldiers, nor the British people nor the British government, which had previously received the same assistance in the matter of food and munitions that they received afterwards, but it gave to a small number of London capitalists the privilege of escaping Canadian taxation on their choice commercial investments. Here is another quotation from the Minister of Finance:
We have realized for some time that the accumulation of sterling balances .	.	. was
appropriate only as an interim or transitory form of assistance. It involved the growing up of what was nominally a demand liability by Britain to Canada, the future of which was bound to involve uncertainties, particularly as the amount grew far beyond anything which could be repaid by Britain in Canadian dollars, except perhaps over a very long period of time.
Then he went on:
The indefinite growth of this obligation, if permitted to continue for years, would have led to the existence after the war of what would be in effect a huge and unmanageable war debt owed by Britain to Canada.
If Britain could not manage a war debt owed to Canada, how could the dominion government manage a huge war debt owed by the Canadian taxpayers? The measure was praised by several parties in the house, and was opposed by some. I was persistent in asking for detailed information, and on May 10 of last year I said:
If we want information it is not only with regard to what has been done in the past; it is for the purpose of having a guarantee for the future. It is the only check we have, now that responsibility is taken out of our hands.

Apparently much more was financed than was purchased or accounted for. He also gave a statement of how those Canadian dollars were obtained by Britain and the rest of the sterling area, which included two "balancing items" of $17 million and $41 million, respectively, and explained that these were "apparent errors and omissions due in part to the use of preliminary figures." I was far from being appeased and said:
Mutual Aid

Once more I challenge the leader of the opposition, the ex-leader of the opposition and everybody to your left-
Mr. Casselman: Challenge your own side.
Mr. Pouliot: -I will ask them why they have not complained of the fact that the Bank of Canada cannot reach a balance in the account-
Some hon. members: Order.
Mr. Pouliot: We are discussing lend-lease legislation. How is it that at page 5 of the statement tabled yesterday by the minister there is $17 million for which it is impossible to render account by reason of the mix-up that exists at the Bank of Canada for the calendar year 1942, and $41 million for the year 1942-43? This is relevant to the bill. How is it that the ex-leader of the opposition with his magnifying glass did not say anything about it, although he rises so easily and is always so full of indignation? Why does he not support me-
Some hon. members: Order.
Then the minister said:
On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, we must either have the rule established or disregard it, that the discussion must be relevant to the item before the committee. The item under discussion is section 2 of the bill, which is an interpretative section defining certain terms. It is quite within the right of any hon. member to object to those definitions or ask questions about them, advocate other definitions or point out undesirable results that would follow from defining those terms in that way. But I submit it is not in order to deal with documents that were placed before the house, not under this item at all but as a matter of accounting for the disposition of last year's billion-dollar gift.
There was some argument, and finally I said that I hoped the discussion would be resumed later. Why should anyone worry? The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) had informed the house the day before that-
... we maintain a large staff of chartered accountants in England to determine exactly what the costs are.
There was also the united nations mutual aid bill, which was introduced on May 6,1943. The hon. member for Riehelieu-Vercheres, spoke on that occasion, and spoke well. The hon. member for Gaspe also made a good speech. Some members voted for, and others voted against. The hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains moved the six months' hoist. The hon. member for Bellechasse and the financial critic of the New Democracy group made very able speeches on that occasion. The speech of the hon. member for Bellechasse was well reasoned, and he stated in it that Canada had a right to expect something in return for mutual aid.
Now, sir, we have the same thing. We have protested about financing which we believe is wrong. We protest, too, against the wrong interpretation given to our remarks. At the present time we are fighting the cause of the

taxpayer. We do it in all earnestness, and believe the time has come when we must protect ourselves by asking for some security, or at least for some acknowledgment, from countries receiving assistance from Canada. That was the view even of some members who voted for the bill.
Opinions are free. I will stand by the will of the majority; I will respect it. But to say that anyone is a bad Canadian because he does not swallow every piece of legislation brought forward by the financial wizards of the Department of Finance, is going too far. It is not fair for any member to cast aspersions upon or to impute motives to other members who protest against unsound financing.
It is presented in a strange way. I remember that at the time of the election of the Minister of Justice in Quebec East the people were put under the impression that it was a gift, something like that received at Christmas time. They were told that gifts were sent overseas, and that we were not sending money. Reasoning like that is childish. The money comes from the pockets of the Canadian people, and it is a mortgage on the future generation. That is the money with which all those goods are purchased and delivered. In order to be fair to the future generation, in order to alleviate their burdens and to give them an opportunity to start business as most of our fellow Canadians have done before the war, we should have acknowledgments for what Canada has done for other countries.
Apparently it is most unpatriotic to ask for them. Who knows who will be at the head of government in Great Britain after the war? Who knows if shadow governments will still be in office when the war is over and when Europe is liberated? We have seen what has happened in connection with Yugoslavia. That country had a government in Cairo, and then another one was established in Yugoslavia. The government in Cairo, which had the support of the British government for a time, was afterwards denied that support. No one knows with whom we shall be dealing after the war is over, when we have treaties and agreements to sign with other nations in the world. Therefore it is difficult to leave it at that, and to trust those who have assumed the task of forming governments to remember what Canada has done for those countries. I shall not' insist any longer. I have said what I wanted to say. I find the principle of the legislation unsound, although the purpose may be good.

Mutual Aid

I was referring to the fact that in another bill before the house there is a clause providing for independence of the members of the board from the particular industry concerned. I was referring in that case to the bill to amend the Aeronautics Act, and I suggested that in the bill now before us there should be a similar provision so that the members of this board would be independent financially of the industries interested in the work which this board and corporation will carry on.
In the reply which the minister made-it was only a partial answer because the discussion was interrupted to take up another item of business-he referred to the desirability of securing the services of men who have had experience in a particular line. I believe it is well known, Mr. Chairman, that we have never objected to that principle, namely, the securing of the services of men who know the business involved. Throughout the course of the war we have objected to the dollar-a-year-man principle, but we have not objected to calling upon men to do the jobs of which they are capable. We have objected to what we regard as an expensive policy, namely, the employing of men for a dollar a year, with the result that they have to maintain their private business connections. We contend that for the full protection of the interests of the people as a whole, men directing such important works as have had to be directed during the course of the war and the men who will now direct this important task should be independent of the interests of private enterprise and private business. As hon. members know, we have objected for several years now to the dollar-a-year-man policy with respect to the controls and measures by which sections of the war economy have been run. We now object to the carrying over of that principle into the post-war period in so far as the setup of this board is concerned.
I repeat that in my view there should be in this bill, in either section 10 or section 11, a provision for the independence of the board comparable with the position of the board to which I referred last night under the bill to amend the Aeronautics Act.

This particular clause is wide open and I think that before the committee adopts this clause it should have more information from the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply as to the entire personnel of both the allocations committee and the War Assets Corporation. We should see to it that they are free and independent, because the asset that they w'ill handle when the war is over is an asset that belongs to the Canadian people as a whole, and the government in power today is the custodian of that property. Not only is it the obligation of the government to the people to see that the committee are free and independent and that their duties and responsibilities are clearly defined in the bill, but the government should also place in the hands of that committee some definite instructions with regard to the utilization of the assets they are to handle in the future economy of the country.
I consider this whole matter a very important part of our whole post-war programme, and before I am prepared, as one member of the committee, to allow the bill to go through I want more definite and specific information on the asset as it now stands and as to what agreements or understandings the government has with the people who own the land where the plant and equipment are now located. I was going to cite the experience of that barracks because definitely that committee will not have any say in the disposing of that particular property, since it has already been disposed of by agreement with the company that own the land. There is a first option, and when it is taken over, the soldier coming back from the war is not permitted any of the lumber or of the building to provide a roof for himself and his family.
Progress reported.
